item.title: Bills learn from past mistakes in victory over Texans
item.description: After dropping two games in two seasons at Reliant Stadium, the Bills made a major change that helped them to victory
item.content:encoded:
Not much had gone right for the Buffalo Bills when playing at the Houston Texans over the last twenty years. Whether it was NRG Stadium or Reliant Stadium, the Bills had a Houston problem, as they had lost six straight decisions in Houston. I fact, Buffalo had only won twice—once in the Texans’ inaugural season in 2002 and then again in 2006—when playing the Texans in their home stadium.

So it was especially encouraging to see the Bills emerge with a 36-31 win yesterday to open the 2026 season, slaying some demons in a house of horrors for the franchise throughout the 24-year tenure of the Houston football club. Plenty of things went Buffalo’s way on Sunday, including two offensive fumbles that were recovered by the Bills and a Josh Allen fourth-quarter chuck that Kamari Lassiter dropped in the end zone just one play before the game-winning touchdown pass. Those lucky instances are things that right, but there were plenty of things in Buffalo’s control that went right for the team, as well.

One of the biggest issues the Bills had in their previous losses to the Houston was with protection—namely, they couldn’t keep Allen upright. In last year’s 23-19 loss at Houston, Allen took a career-high eight sacks. While some of those sacks were on him for holding the ball too long, there were too many instances where a four-man Houston rush easily overwhelmed a five-man Buffalo protection scheme. When that five-man look still didn’t work, the Bills offered little in the way of changing their plan throughout the contest.

On Sunday, though, the protection scheme looked much different. Buffalo still stuck with some five-man looks, but they varied their protections to keep the Houston edge rushers guessing. Sometimes, they doubled Danielle Hunter and used a tight end to chip Will Anderson. Other times, they did the opposite. They even used wideouts to chip, which we saw work to success on the game’s final play.

It was DJ Moore who chipped Hunter on the game’s final play, helping the keep Spencer Brown in a good position to keep Allen upright. That chip from Moore led to a delayed release into his route, which safety Calen Bullock definitely saw as he cheated just a bit to Moore’s side. That gave Allen the window to chuck a “horseshoe,” as he called it postgame, that Joshua Palmer caught for a game-winning 34-yard score.

Color analyst Ross Tucker said multiple times on the broadcast that teams need to “think players, not plays” in big situations. With Houston likely following that mantra by cheating towards Moore, it gave the Bills and Josh Allen an opening to hit an unlikely hero in Palmer across the field. Had the Bills and their offensive coaching staff not made a conscious decision to change their protection scheme entering this game, giving their offensive linemen help against a ferocious Texans pass rush, that split-second might have been the difference in an incomplete pass or worse. And what we saw was the winning score.

Credit to head coach Joe Brady, offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael Jr., and offensive line coach Pat Meyer for changing their approach in Sunday’s win.

item.title: Falcons may lose DL Da’Shawn Hand for the season
item.description: The veteran run stopper may be on the shelf for the rest of 2026, and that would be a big loss.
item.content:encoded:
The Atlanta Falcons have lost Jalon Walker for the season, seen James Pearce Jr. suspended for eight games, started their third-string quarterback, and lost a road game featuring awful turnovers, tons of penalties, and missed field goals. We are only one week into the season and struggling to keep the vibes positive, and today’s news is not going to help.

Defensive lineman Da’Shawn Hand, who only played seven snaps in Week 1 before exiting with a knee injury, may miss the rest of the 2026 season with a torn quad. Hand was expected be a key piece of this run defense up front, and his loss would be a major blow to a promising defensive line.

Hand was one of the bigger (pun intended) signings of the offseason, and was added with an eye on improving an often shaky 2025 run defense. While the Falcons did a nice job in Week 1 with Brandon Dorlus, LaCale London, Gervon Dexter, and Maason Smith all playing well, that’s a four man rotation and none of them have the track record against the run that Hand does. Atlanta will almost certainly add either Zach Harrison or Zacch Pickens to the active roster and may scour free agency for more additions, simply because any attrition at all will leave this team perilously thin up front.

We’ll have to hope for some miraculous good news, but given the way the season has gone already, I’m not expecting it. Devastated for Da’Shawn Hand.

item.title: Fantasy Football Waiver Wire Week 1: Target Caleb Douglas and Kaelon Black
item.description: Dolphins rookie Caleb Douglas looks like his team's WR1 making him the top waiver wire add of the week. Fellow rookie Kaelon Black has also carved out a role as Christian McCaffrey's backup and then some.
item.content:encoded:
Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season is in the books, Monday Night Football aside. That means it's time for the first run of waivers. Every play in this article is available in at least half of all Yahoo leagues. Players within each position are generally ordered by FAAB/waiver priority.

▶ Quarterback

Tyler Shough, Saints

The Saints ran 81 offensive plays in their Week 1 shootout with the Lions. They ran 13 more plays than any other team, though making it deep into overtime certainly helps. Kellen Moore dialed up the fastest offense in the NFL last year. They remained a fast-paced unit in Week 1, and their pass rate over expected went from -2.9% in 2025 to +4.1% on Sunday. If that holds, this will be the highest passing volume team of the season. Shough struggled mightily in the first half versus Detroit but turned things around late in the game, resulting in a slightly positive EPA per dropback. That plus the passing volume is enough to get him in the QB1 mix next week.

Bryce Young, Panthers

I will admit that I’m skeptical Young can sustain his elite Week 1 showing, but it's hard to oversell how good the results were. He threw for 361 yards and three scores while also punching in a fourth on the ground. The Bears’ defense played poorly and their offense nearly scored 60, creating the perfect environment to force the Panthers to score points of their own. That won’t happen every week. On the other hand, Young ranked eighth in EPA per dropback, ninth in CPOE, and seventh in PFF passing grade, pending Monday's game. It was a great showing from him. He’s entering his fourth season and is working with a pair of ascending wideouts in Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker. Maybe this is his breakout year.

Malik Willis, Dolphins

Willis comes in a tier or two below the previous two streaming quarterbacks. As expected, the Dolphins were extremely run-heavy in Week 1, logging a -3.7% PROE. He attempted just 27 passes, was sacked five times, and threw one interception. On the plus side, Willis rushed six times for 39 yards and a touchdown. Pending Monday Night Football, he had the third-most scrambles in Week 1. Willis’s struggles as a passer will prevent him from cracking the QB1 ranks, but he’s a fine QB2 option.

▶ Running Back

Kaelon Black, 49ers

The 49ers have a locked-in RB2. Jordan James was a healthy scratch while Black out-carried Christian McCaffrey 14-10. This is unprecedented usage for McCaffrey’s backup.

#49ers RB Kaelon Black finished with 14 carries for 65 yards. Christian McCaffrey had 10 carries for 68 yards.

Including playoffs, this is the first time that a 49er had more rushing attempts than McCaffrey in a game that CMC played in (and didn't exit due to injury) since 2022…

— Nick Wagoner (@nwagoner) September 11, 2026

McCaffrey was reportedly dealing with cramps in a game halfway across the globe, so it’s probably safe to assume he will return to leading the team in carries next week. Still, his efficiency numbers cratered in 2025 and he looked phenomenal in Week 1, so a touches split might make sense for him. Black could have some standalone value going forward and is the best contingent bet on waivers. In terms of FAAB, Black may ultimately get over-hyped. If CMC does flip him in carries next week, he’s barely a viable FLEX option. This is roughly a 20% spend for me.

Tyler Allgeier, Cardinals

Allgeier out-carried Jeremiyah Love 17-11, though both backs got red zone opportunities and Love was the only one to cash in. Love also saw four targets to Allgeier’s two. With Love still working through his preseason ankle injury on Sunday, it made sense for the Cardinals to ease his workload, especially in a game they inexplicably won. The Cardinals get brutal matchups with the Seahawks and 49ers coming up, so it’s hard to imagine Allgeier pushing anywhere close to 20 touches in either of his next two games. He will be a two-down RB4 for Week 2, but that might be a useful waiver wire add for some fantasy managers.

Braelon Allen, Jets

Allen’s 10 carries for 40 scoreless yards deserve a mention, even if he’s not on the fantasy radar for Week 2. Breece Hall ran the ball 22 times, earned four targets, and saw all of the goal line work. Allen was only targeted once. The Jets handled business against the Titans in Week 1 but are still 4.5-point dogs to the Packers next week. Assuming Vegas is correct, there will be way fewer carries to go around in this backfield. Allen is the clear handcuff to Hall but nothing more.

Kendre Miller, Saints

Miller split carries evenly with Travis Etienne in Week 1. Both backs saw nine attempts and Miller was the one who punched in a red zone score. Even third-string running back CJ Donaldson got in the mix for two carries plus two targets. This backfield is only going to get messier when Alvin Kamara returns, which should happen next week. Miller is worth an add in deeper leagues, but his value will likely take a hit in Week 2.

Week 1 Stock Up, Stock Down: Bear returns
Rivers McCown looks at four players who saw their fantasy football stock go up and four players who saw their fantasy football stock decline from Week 1’s early returns.
  • Rivers McCown,

▶ Wide Receiver

Caleb Douglas, Dolphins

Hot off an electric training camp, Douglas drew the start and ran a route on 86 percent of Willis's dropbacks. He earned 26 percent target share and a monstrous 40 percent first-read target share. Douglas turned this role into five catches for 94 yards. Miami’s run-first offense will be an issue for Douglas and the rest of the pass-catchers in the long-run, but a Day Two rookie is the focal point of a team’s passing attack in Week 1. That is a clear target off the waiver wire, regardless of how many times the team throws. Douglas is the No. 1 FAAB priority this week, slightly ahead of Black.

Deebo Samuel, 49ers

De’Zhaun Stribling is expected to miss an extended period of time with an ankle injury he suffered in Week 1. Samuel only ran half of the routes in Week 1, splitting the WR2 role with Demarcus Robinson. On the plus side, Samuel tied Mike Evans at seven targets and posted a 6/48/1 receiving line. He also turned his lone carry into a 12-yard gain. Samuel’s route share should grow with Stribling out and he already looked good on a per-route basis. Samuel is barely available in over half of Yahoo leagues, but he’s shaping up to be a WR3/4 if you can get him.

Devaughn Vele, Saints

With Jordyn Tyson on IR, Vele took over the No. 2 role on a Saints team that was about to pass more than any other squad in the league. He played extremely well, turning his nine targets and 70 air yards into a 7/69/1 receiving line. Vele ran a route on 92 percent of Shough’s dropbacks. He isn’t the most exciting add, but Vele looks like a WR4 in another potential shootout with the Ravens next week.

Tre Harris, Chargers

Ladd McConkey went down with a chest injury in the third quarter. Harris and Quentin Johnston each logged a 77 percent route rate. Both players saw six targets, though neither did much with them. Harris was nominally more productive, catching three of his looks for 20 yards. Harris posted absurd numbers in college and was drafted in the second round. He didn’t do much as a rookie, but a McConkey injury could clear the way for a second-year breakout.

Dontayvion Wicks, Eagles

As expected, Wicks operated as the Eagles’ No. 2 receiver, running 91 percent of the routes. He was primarily a deep threat. Wicks had an aDOT of 21.8 and was targeted on a measly 13 percent of his routes. He, of course, got home with a 64-yard touchdown on one of his two receptions.

Dontayvion Wicks said postgame that he was actually running a clear-out route on his 64-yard catch vs. WAS.

The ball never came his way when they repped the play in practice.

"It was always just getting out of the way, but you never know with 1 [Hurts.] He might put it up there… pic.twitter.com/CywGtImM6h

— EJ Smith (@EJSmith94) September 14, 2026

Wicks is a good deep threat, but he’s going to be extremely frustrating to roster on a weekly basis.

Kalif Raymond, Bears

The Bears dropped 57 points on Carolina and none of the pass-catchers we care about did better than 63 scoreless yards. That’s because Raymond easily led the team with nine targets, eight catches, and 84 yards. Raymond set a career-high in receptions and posted his best yardage total since 2023. He did so on a pedestrian 58 percent route rate. Raymond did, however, lead the Bears with a 33 percent first read target share. It’s hard to imagine him being their top wideout going forward, but Ben Johnson clearly has a package of plays for the speedster that could make him a viable FLEX play. I wouldn’t spend any FAAB on Raymond, but he’s worth stashing in deep leagues.

▶ Tight End

Dalton Schultz, Texans

Schultz was a mainstay of last year’s waiver wire column and nothing changes one week into 2026. He tied a handful of other tight ends for the second-most targets at his position in Week 1 with eight. That was good for a 21 percent target share, which is actually a three percent increase from his 2025 mark. For the second year in a row, Schultz remains the most boring TE1 you can get off waivers.

Pat Freiermuth, Steelers

Pittsburgh hit us with the Mike McCarthy special in Week 1, logging a pass rate 10 percent above expected. Aaron Rodgers attempted to throw deep, but was once again only successful on his short tosses. He had the fifth-lowest completed air yards per attempt on the week at 3.8. This ultimately creates the perfect environment for tight end production, and McCarthy streamlined the team’s tight end rotation to just one player: Pat Freiermuth. Muth ran 73 percent of the routes in Week 1, making him a strong TE2 option in Week 2.

Mike Gesicki, Bengals

Gesicki turned in a 5/78/1 receiving line in a shootout with the Bucs. That would’ve been his second-best fantasy score of the entire 2025 season and will give him a top-12 finish in Week 1. The downside is that he ran a route on just 46 percent of Joe Burrow’s dropbacks. He led a team with Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins in targets while running fewer than half of the routes. As impressive as that is, I’m not counting on it repeating next week. Gesicki is an interesting stash but not someone who profiles as a weekly starter.

item.title: Grading the Steelers' NFL Week 1 win: T.J. Watt, Alex Highsmith were disruptive
item.description: Mike McCarthy's team showed plenty of encouraging signs against the Falcons, but the running game and offensive line need to improve moving forward.
item.content:encoded:
The Pittsburgh Steelers picked up a 20-13 victory against the Atlanta Falcons on Sept. 13 at Acrisure Stadium. 

On paper, it was a feel-good start to coach Mike McCarthy’s tenure as coach after 19 seasons of Mike Tomlin standing at the helm.  

In practice, it felt at times like the Steelers should have pulled away a lot faster from a Falcons team that was down to its third-string quarterback. 

Here are USA TODAY’s position-by-position grades for the effort from a Steelers perspective. 

Required reading: 3 takeaways as Mike McCarthy transforms Steelers offense in win vs Falcons

Quarterback - A

Aaron Rodgers’ box score line wasn't very pretty – 24 of 40 passing for 221 yards and a touchdown. That’s an inefficient 5.5 yards per attempt that evokes a lot of his results in Arthur Smith’s more conservative offense last season. 

The film will show that he put a lot of downfield passes on target for his receivers. They just didn’t come down with them for one reason or another. (We’ll get to that shortly.)

He looked comfortable back in the McCarthy system that he knows so well from his Green Bay days. He knows where the ball needs to go, and he was not overly reliant on his running backs in the passing game like we was last season, when so much seemed to flow through Kenneth Gainwell. He might not have been playing at quite an MVP level, but that kind of effort will work more weeks than it won’t. 

Running backs - C

It was an unimpressive debut for Rico Dowdle, one of the team’s key offseason acquisitions. He had just eight carries for 15 yards and two catches for six. That’s not good enough for 10 touches. 

Jaylen Warren was a bit better. He had five catches for 27 yards and added 46 yards on 10 carries. That translates to a healthy 4.6 yards per carry average. Seventeen of those yards came on a single late fourth quarter carry, however. Without it, his average would have been 3.2. That better reflects how generally ineffective the group was for the vast majority of the afternoon. 

More: 32 things we learned in NFL Week 1 − just don't ask who the best team is right now

Receivers - C+

We’ll be a bit more generous than perhaps these guys deserve here, given the drops, for a couple of reasons. One, as Rodgers pointed out postgame, the Steelers had a good case for a couple more interference calls than they ultimately received. One along the sideline to DK Metcalf was particularly egregious and justly drew loud boos from the crowd. It’s hard to pile onto them too hard for dropping balls with an inherently higher degree of difficulty attached to them.

The second reason is more important and less whiny: They were open and in position to make plays. That wasn’t true a lot of times late in the Tomlin days. If that can happen consistently in this offense, then we’re betting we won’t be talking about drops nearly as much across a larger sample size. 

It was also encouraging to see Michael Pittman Jr. average nearly 20 yards across his three receptions in his Steelers debut that came at the end of an injury-plagued training camp and preseason. 

Tight ends - B+

Until Pittman made a late catch, Pat Freiermuth was the team’s leading receiver for the afternoon. He still ended up with more catches than anyone else with five. Darnell Washington was solid in his primary role as a blocker, then caught the Falcons napping for a 15-yard catch in the four-minute drill that helped put the game away. 

Offensive line - C

This might be a pass-first offense with Mike McCarthy, but this group still needs to create a lot more holes in the running game than it did. Averaging 2.8 yards per carry will not be enough to keep defenses honest very often. In pass blocking, the group allowed pressures on 12 of Rodgers’ 40 attempts, per Pro Football Focus data. Just one led to a sack, and only one other led to a hit on Rodgers. So at least they kept his person fairly clean. 

More: Cowboys' defensive calamity leads NFL Week 1 winners and losers

Linebackers - A+

It wasn’t just about the huge day for the pass rushers. Yes, T.J. Watt’s interception of Rush and the ensuing touchdown return essentially won the game. And yes, his two sacks – plus a pair from fellow outside linebacker Alex Highsmith – contributed massively to Rush being in a proverbial blender all afternoon.

But it was also great to see Payton Wilson and Patrick Queen step up in run defense on a day that All-Pro Bijan Robinson was lining up in the opposing backfield. Those two had six stops between them, defined by PFF as plays that result in failure for the opposing offense. More of that moving forward would be a key development for this defense in DC Patrick Grahm’s first season. 

Defensive line - B

Cam Heyward batted three of Rush’s passes at the line of scrimmage. It’s one of his underrated skills that’s kept him toward the top of his profession well into his 30s. In the running game, he finished the game with two stops, and fellow starters Derrick Harmon and Keeanu Benton added three and two, respectively. Paired with the linebackers’ production, it was more than enough to keep Robinson mostly bottled up on the ground. He averaged just four yards across his 21 carries. 

Secondary - A

Falcons receivers not named Robinson caught four passes for 53 yards all afternoon. This defense will gladly trade some yards to the running back underneath to keep a lid on opponents. It helped that Rush was the opposing quarterback this time. Drake Maye’s performance next week in New England will probably tell us a lot more about this pass defense unit. Still, it was a good start considering the Steelers played this game without Joey Porter Jr. starting the game and with Jamel Dean getting a bit banged up at times. 

Coaching - B+

Graham's defense flummoxed Rush and contained Robinson to ace its two primary tests for the afternoon. McCarthy's offense looked refreshingly aggressive. It was the change of pace many Steelers fans were hoping for. McCarthy just needs to get the execution squared away moving forward in both the running and passing games.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Grading the Steelers' NFL Week 1 win: T.J. Watt, Alex Highsmith were disruptive

item.title: Steelers PFF grades: Aaron Rodgers gets high marks for downfield looks
item.description: Troy Fautanu tops the list of players who need to show more, starting with a Week 2 matchup against the New England Patriots.
item.content:encoded:
The Pittsburgh Steelers are 1-0 after a 20-13 victory against the Atlanta Falcons on Sept. 13 at Acrisure Stadium. 

The stars played a big part in getting them there. T.J. Watt returned a fourth-quarter interception for a touchdown to provide the game-winning points. Veteran receiver Michael Pittman Jr. – the headliner of the team’s 2026 free agent class – caught three passes for 58 yards. And Alex Highsmith knifed through Atlanta blockers to record two sacks of his own. 

Add it all up, and the positives were plentiful for first-year coach Mike McCarthy in his debut. 

Here’s a look at some of the highlights and lowlights through the eyes of Pro Football Focus evaluators, who study every play on film to grade each player individually. For context, players are graded on a 0-100 scale.

Required reading: 3 takeaways as Mike McCarthy transforms Steelers offense in win vs Falcons

Aaron Rodgers (80.5)

The number that jumps off the page for the future Hall of Fame quarterback is an average depth of target (ADOT) of 10.1 yards. In former offensive coordinator Arthur Smith’s system a year ago, he averaged just 6.6 yards per throw. That was a career low. He also recorded the fastest average time to throw of his career at 2.60 seconds. Sunday, that figure was 2.84. McCarthy is giving him the time and encouragement to look down the field and resemble something much closer to the Rodgers of his MVP-winning days with the Packers. He may not be quite that good physically anymore, robbing him of some of the pocket maneuverability he once had. Still, Steelers fans will likely love seeing him a bit more in his element than he was under Arthur Smith. Especially if receivers like DK Metcalf and Roman Wilson can start actually coming down with more passes than they did Sunday. 

T.J. Watt (92.3)

If he keeps playing like this, he might have one more defensive player of the year award in him with the Packers’ Micah Parsons and the Rams’ Myles Garrett both injured this season. It wasn’t just the game-winning interception return that was encouraging, even as it was clearly the exclamation point. It was two sacks. It was four total pressures of Falcons quarterback Cooper Rush. It was four stops, which PFF defines as plays that result in failure for an opposing offense on a given down. Those helped contain Atlanta star Bijan Robinson to just 83 yards across his 21 carries for the afternoon. Watt was everywhere, a stark departure from last season when he had just seven sacks and 49 pressures, his worst total in a healthy season since his rookie campaign in 2017. 

Troy Fautanu (44.4)

The early returns on his transition back to left tackle weren’t promising. The veteran in his third season allowed three pressures of Rodgers – two hurries and a hit. That was the most of any Steelers offensive lineman. And his run blocking score was an ugly 37.4. None of the other Steelers regulars scored worse than a 55.8 in that category, even as the team averaged an inefficient 2.8 yards per carry. Fautanu hasn’t protected a quarterback’s blindside since before lefty Michael Penix Jr. arrived at Washington in 2023, so some growing pains were to be expected here. Still, had former teammate Broderick Jones turned in this type of performance, he’d be getting crushed for it. So it’s only fair to note that Fautanu needs to be better. 

Jamel Dean (78.6) and Jaquan Brisker (78.1)

Playing without injured teammate Joey Porter Jr., the defense’s key offseason acquisitions were great. Between them, they were challenged just three times by Rush. They allowed a pair of receptions for 27 yards, but Briker picked off the third pass to set up the offense’s only touchdown of the day. Top Atlanta receiver Drake London managed just two catches for 29 yards, so that’s a credit to Dean, who overcame being banged up for portions of this game as well.  

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Steelers PFF grades: Aaron Rodgers gets high marks for downfield looks

item.title: Jacksonville Jaguars Winners and Losers From Week 1: Jags Stomp Lowly Browns In All Three Phases
item.description: Victory Monday feels oh so good when you handle business.
item.content:encoded:
I truly don’t know of a much better way to start a season than what the Jaguars did on Sunday.

Against the god-awful Cleveland Browns, the Jacksonville Jaguars did far more than handle business in their 34-10 season-opener win. It’s now 2-0 in season openers in Duval County for Liam Coen and the vibes couldn’t be higher.

When you have a win where arguably the worst play for your team is allowing a long kickoff return that didn’t go for a touchdown, resulting in just three points, you probably played pretty well. That’s how it seemed on Sunday.

No real losers this week as the Jaguars ride high as the only AFC South team to win their opener, starting the season 1-0.

WINNERS
The Jaguars

Everyone’s a winner collectively from yesterday’s game. Sometimes you just need to handle business, not play with your food and win a game outright. The Jags did that in all three phases.

The offense scored on its first four drives, not having to punt until the final drive of the first half. The defense grabbed a pick on Cleveland’s first drive and forced about two dozen more fumbles throughout the game to go along with five sacks. Special teams did its job with a pair of long field goals from Cam Little and got some nice returns from Ameer Abdullah and Parker Washington. Handle business and move on.

The decreased stadium capacity was a little strange and the heat definitely impacted the crowd, but the Jags fans showed up like they always do to see the team off right to start the season. We can’t play the Browns every week but it’s a start. On to Denver.

Trevor Lawrence

Coen was asked postgame about the importance of starting Trevor Lawrence fast this season in the second season of this offense. The head coach said he and his staff were more intentional about working earlier in the week on the script. It paid off big time.

Had it not been for some mammoth games by Caleb Williams (the Chicago variant) or Tyler Shough, Lawrence might have had the best quarterbacking day in the league on Sunday.

Lawrence went a solid 18-23 for 245 yards and four touchdowns. He was sacked just once and was turnover free. The offense moved at will with Lawrence slinging it. It was smooth, his throws were layered beautifully and it just looked all around clean. Juxtaposed to whatever the hell Deshaun Watson was doing, it made Lawrence look even that much better.

The quarterback has a clear trust in every offensive weapon he has, with nine different guys catching at least one pass. The most catches on that list though did belong to… 

Parker Washington

Hey look, Parker Washington is actually good and it wasn’t just a one season thing. Maybe they should have paid him. 

In all seriousness, Washington was perhaps the best non-Lawrence player on the field yesterday with five catches for 83 yards and his leaping opening drive touchdown. He looks like a legit WR1 after just a game. Maybe the best part about Washington is that his newfound superstardom finds guys like Jakobi Meyers (two catches, 40 yards, one score) and Brian Thomas Jr. (three catches, 40 yards) that much more open. It all works in tandem. Sunday was a testament to that.

Chop Wood. Carry Water. Catch touchdowns.

Rookies

Another guy who benefitted from the Washington hype train was rookie wide receiver Josh Cameron, who caught a touchdown in his first NFL game.

Cameron looks the part through one game: a two catch, 20 yard and a score performance. His big frame is clearly something Jacksonville wants to take advantage of early and often. 

Nate Boerkircher hauled in a pass as well, highlighting another rookie who flashed in spurts Sunday. Brenton Strange led the tight end room in “moments” so to speak, but the rookie Boerkircher did his job. As did rookie guard Emmanuel Pregnon, who got the start up front. At least offensively, the early returns look just fine for the rooks.

Defense

It probably doesn’t need to be stated just how horrific the Browns are, but the Jags defense had a lot to do with that.

Travon Walker AND Josh Hines-Allen each walked away with 1.5 sacks. Foye Oluokun had a pick that resulted in a touchdown drive. Ventrell Miller looked like prime Brian Urlacher, leading the team with 10 tackles, two tackles for loss and a sack. Travis Hunter played both sides and played well.

Those are your cornerstone guys who made the big plays all day long. You cannot ask for anything more.

There is something to be said that Anthony Campanile stayed in Jacksonville and got another season with what was a good defense last year. All three levels of the defense played well all day long and coach Camp should be getting a lot of praise for that fact.

Obligatory Cam Little Mention

Little was solid again Sunday, connecting on his two kicks of 47 yards and 40 yards. I would’ve loved to see him actually make a tackle on that long kick return but oh well. Ross Matiscik laid the boom in his place later anyway.

Ameer Abdullah

I would’ve guessed that if I was mentioning Abdullah in any capacity after a Jags game, it would be because everyone else played so badly and I was grasping at straws. But not so fast.

The Jags RB3-ish actually looked really good in his limited time. He had four carries for 32 yards and amassed 59 total kick return yards. He’s a veteran player and for what the Jags seemingly are going to use him for, he should be great. Credit to him.

LOSERS

Deshaun Watson

This dude flat out sucks, holy mother of Mary. The demons that follow Watson around and speak ancient phrases into his ears were working overtime Sunday. That first interception he threw was perfect timing for the defense. See ya next week.

Who do you think was the big winner from the Jags Week 1 win? Want to talk more on how well Lawrence played? Comment down below and we will see you right back here for the team’s Week 2 matchup next Sunday at the Denver Broncos.

item.title: Titans vs. Eagles opening odds
item.description: No shot I’d put any money on the Titans
item.content:encoded:
I was traveling yesterday and didn’t get home until midnight, so I didn’t get to watch the game or write anything about it. It might be better that way. Yesterday’s game was nothing short of depressing. It’s hard to point to a game on the schedule right now that it feels like the Tennessee Titans have an actual chance of winning.

This week is certainly not a game the Titans have a chance of winning. They opened as a 7-point underdog at FanDuel Sportsbook to the Philadelphia Eagles. I’m pretty surprised that isn’t a double-digit number. The Titans showed nothing on Sunday that gives me any confidence that they can stay within a touchdown of the Eagles.

All offseaosn, I preached the importance of staying paitent with this team. Now, I need someone that can talk me off the ledge. item.title: Mike Vrabel defends Patriots’ offensive game plan against Seahawks
item.description: The Patriots scored only 10 points in their season-opening loss.
item.content:encoded:
After struggling in the Super Bowl, the New England Patriots offense was hopeful to turn things around in its rematch with the Seattle Seahawks defense in Week 1. While the game as a whole was much more competitive, the end result was still disappointing.

The Patriots finished with just 10 points on the day, turned the ball over three times, and were plagued by some of the same issues that already haunted them back on Super Sunday. The game was there for the taking, but Drake Maye’s third interception of the day sealed it in the home team’s favor, which came away with a 13-10 victory over the reigning AFC champions.

In the aftermath of the loss and New England’s disappointing outing, offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels found himself the subject of criticism for what was seen as a fairly conservative game plan. However, head coach Mike Vrabel defended the plan on Monday.

“I don’t look at things as conservative. That’s what we felt like was best against this defense,” Vrabel said during an appearance on WEEI’s The Greg Hill Show.

“We didn’t hit some things and you have to be able to run the football against split safety defense. That’s no secret. You don’t play split safety defense to stop the run; they play it to not give up big plays. We tried to hit some shots down the field. We threw it to the running backs a couple times for 12 or 15 yards when they were all off there, and on the interception should have thrown it to the back again for a third time. You just can’t get bored doing things right. If it’s not there it’s not there.”

Through three quarters, the Patriots had performed decently against one of the NFL’s best defenses. They were up 10-3 and managed to move the ball even after losing star wide receiver A.J. Brown to what was later diagnosed as a high-ankle sprain. New England took its first snap of the fourth quarter — a 1-yard Corey Kiner run — in Seattle territory and with a chance of adding to its lead.

From that point on, however, things went downhill. Drake Maye threw an interception on the very next play while attempting to hit Romeo Doubs deep on the play Vrabel was referencing; this turnover was a turning point in the contest and opened the floodgates.

The Seahawks scored the game-tying touchdown five plays later, while Maye threw another pick on the next possession. Seattle added three more points off of that giveaway, which was then followed by the Patriots driving deep into their opponent’s territory only to be denied on another, game-ending INT.

Could a different game plan have changed things and let the Patriots offense perform at the same level as others around the NFL in Week 1? Not in Vrabel’s estimation.

“Every game is different, every defense is different,” he said. “We all sit down, we game-plan. Josh game-plans with his staff; each guy has an area. I’ll sit in with those. I think to look and say, ‘Well, this guy, this team put up number…’ — we didn’t win the game.”

item.title: Sean McVay Meter: Fans’ confidence in coach after Week 1
item.description: Are you concerned about the direction that Sean McVay has the Rams going?
item.content:encoded:
One game does not define a season, but Rams fans have every right to feel frustrated after what unfolded in Melbourne.

The Los Angeles Rams entered Week 1 with high expectations, only to deliver a disappointing performance against the San Francisco 49ers. When a team struggles in multiple areas, the head coach is naturally going to face questions, and Sean McVay is no exception.

McVay has earned the benefit of the doubt throughout his tenure in Los Angeles. His track record includes a Super Bowl championship, multiple playoff appearances and a reputation as one of the NFL’s best offensive minds. However, expectations have changed. Rams fans are no longer simply hoping for playoff football —they expect this team to win a championship come February.

Sean McVay Fan Confidence Meter

  • 9-10 — Unshakable
  • 7-8 — Strong
  • 5-6 — Cautiously Optimistic
  • 3-4 — Frustrated
  • 1-2 — Crisis

The Week 1 performance could test the patience of a fan base that believes the Rams have enough talent to make a deep postseason run. Questions about game planning, execution and adjustments will inevitably lead back to McVay.

There also could also be lingering frustration surrounding how the team handled Myles Garrett’s knee situation. If Garrett’s knee issues were already a concern in July, some fans may question why the situation wasn’t addressed more aggressively before the regular season. Seeing an important player deal with the consequences now can make those earlier decisions easier to scrutinize.

The season is far from over, but the Sean McVay Meter has already moved. Whether it is a temporary reaction to one bad performance or the beginning of deeper concerns will depend heavily on how McVay and the Rams respond in Week 2.

item.title: NFC West Recap: 49ers in first place after Week 1; the Rams are not
item.description: It’s only one game, but the 49ers’ one game was a divisional one, and the win puts them in first place.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to the weekly NFC West recap. For those of you new to the program, we’ll do a rundown of how the San Francisco 49ers are faring against their other NFC West rivals and any news from those games that might be noteworthy.

And we begin things with who is in the lead. First, all the NFC West teams won this weekend—except the Los Angeles Rams. Of those three, the 49ers are in first place after Week 1. Divisional games are considered a “game and a half” in terms of value, and since that was the only NFC West game this weekend, the 49ers start out on top.

Don’t get too excited; it is Week 1 after all. Last year the 49ers beat the Seahawks in Seattle, and then the season happened. Regardless, starting the season with not just a win, but a divisional win can only help in January tiebreakers. Everyone else? Whatever.

San Francisco 49ers (1-0)/Los Angeles Rams (0-1)

Oh, you know what time it is. It’s time to RAM IT.

I don’t know about you, but I really, really enjoyed that 27-7 thumping the 49ers handed the Rams on Thursday. Obviously, just because it’s the Rams, it’s already enjoyable, but seeing the 49ers look so crisp and efficient while the Rams look the opposite (especially after all the offseason hype) brings a lot of optimism about what the 49ers could do. Just stay healthy. Please, 49ers?

Speaking of health, the 49ers got nailed by the injury bug twice. Tight end Jake Tonges went down with what was later said to be MCL-related and “not good.” A bit less severe was wide receiver De’Zhaun Stribling, who went down with what is speculated to be a grade 2 deltoid sprain. This is the first time I learned the ankle has a “deltoid,” but leave it to the 49ers to teach me about every ligament in the human body you can sprain or tear. Stribling is expected to be out for at least a month, and surgery is on the table. Given that this is his rookie season and the 49ers are already dealing with the absence of Ricky Pearsall, we can all hope Stribling gets healthy sooner rather than later. Things could have been worse; when you see a player carted off the field (which happened to Stribling), it usually indicates something devastating.

Making any declarations from Week 1 is a terrible idea, and I’m sure the 49ers might have some challenges in Week 2, even against the Miami Dolphins, but if they can stay healthy, I don’t see why someone can’t see them as a threat to the NFC (not just the West).

As for the Rams, again, it’s Week 1. When they play the 49ers in Week 14, they will have Aaron Donald (and whether he’s still got it or not is left to be determined), and Myles Garrett will probably be a much different player than the one who laid a goose egg on the stat sheet Thursday.

That is, of course, if the Rams have Garrett back by then. It came out Sunday that the defensive lineman will undergo knee surgery and head to injured reserve. The minimum is four games, but there’s no timeline on when Garrett will be back on the roster. Not good, especially when the Rams have some tough games coming up.

Outside of the defense, some might think Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford might be on the “decline” after one game. Just because they brought in the backup to protect Stafford from getting blasted in garbage time doesn’t mean anything. We’ve also seen Stafford play bad games before, so Week 1 in Australia doesn’t indicate anything. Should Stafford be a bit less efficient this year, the Rams have plenty of talent on offense around him to prevent that side of the ball from taking a nosedive.

Seattle Seahawks (1-0)

The defending Super Bowl champs began their season against the New England Patriots. The first points weren’t scored until six minutes into the second quarter. And things imploded in the fourth quarter, when Drake Maye threw three straight interceptions that led to points and a 13-10 win for the Seahawks.

It wasn’t all roses for the Seahawks, however. Quarterback Sam Darnold left with an injury to his hip five plays into the game, leaving Drew Lock to fill in. Darnold is expected to miss some time. It’s not a fracture, so at the moment it’s not thought to be season-ending, but he will miss some time.

Lock went 16-of-22, 187 yards for one touchdown. Simply having zero interceptions means he was far more efficient than Maye. The Seahawks don’t have a favorable schedule the next few weeks, with the Arizona Cardinals, Washington Commanders, and Los Angeles Chargers coming up, so if Darnold is going to be resting up, Seahawks fans will be hoping Lock doesn’t tip things over.

Arizona Cardinals (1-0)

Sure, the 49ers win over the Rams was a surprise, but there was no bigger surprise than the Cardinals beating the Los Angeles Chargers. The Chargers were favored by 9.5 points. Or were the Cardinals favored? I really don’t know because the final score was 26-14, Cardinals. Looks like those points wouldn’t be needed. The game was relatively close until the fourth quarter. That was when stuff like this happened:

The Cardinals have Jacoby Brissett at quarterback, but the Chargers have Justin Herbert. And for a team like the Cardinals, you’d think Herbert would do better than going 17 for 27 and handing the game away with a costly interception.

Then again, Herbert’s offensive line was not helping him at all as the Cardinals’ pass rush was in the backfield on the regular. The stat sheet says Herbert was sacked three times, but it sure felt like a lot more.

The win puts the Cardinals into a tiebreaker with Seattle—one we aren’t going to break down in Week 1. Are the Cardinals better than we thought? Again, it’s Week 1. We’ll see how they do next week in their first NFC West matchup.

Onto Week 2

If the 49ers are going to deal with any jet lag in their return from Australia, it at least will be against the Miami Dolphins at Levi’s Stadium. The Dolphins didn’t have a great Sunday, losing to the Las Vegas Raiders 27-13. That’s the start of what many think will be a bad season.

The Seahawks and Cardinals will be giving us our second NFC West matchup of the season. I want to say the Seahawks won’t have trouble with this, but after Sunday’s upset—and Seattle’s issues with their quarterback—who knows. The game is in Arizona, so take what you will from that.

The Rams will host the New York Giants on Monday Night Football. While we shouldn’t hold our breath, a Giants victory here would open the floodgates for chaos next Tuesday with the Rams, an anointed “super team” in the offseason, starting 0-2. The Giants didn’t have many issues against the Dallas Cowboys, but the Rams are a massive difficulty spike over the Cowboys.

TIE–2nd: Seattle Seahawks; Next: at Arizona Cardinals

item.title: An All-22 review of Jadarian Price’s Seahawks debut vs. Patriots
item.description: Jadarian Price shines in a limited debut as Seattle’s rookie class waits for its chance to contribute.
item.content:encoded:
I’ve missed writing this weekly column. As a Seattle Seahawks fan and someone who loves the draft, one of the things I look forward to most is getting to study how Seattle’s rookies perform once the games actually count.

Unfortunately — or perhaps fortunately, and I’ll explain why later — there isn’t much tape to work with from this season opener. We had just 24 snaps from the rookie class to analyze.

So, let’s take a look at some of the key plays from the game.

All data used in this article was taken from PFF.

Jadarian Price, Running Back — 24 snaps

Price carried the ball 10 times for 52 yards, good for a 5.2-yard average. Overall, he showed good vision, played with a strong attitude and displayed more explosiveness and straight-line speed than I expected coming into the season. At this point, it looks like the praise he received throughout Hard Knocks was legitimate.

This might be the snap that gives Price the clearest indication of what he still needs to improve, although there is nothing alarming here. Seattle appears to be running a Duo concept, a gap-scheme run that uses vertical double teams at the line of scrimmage while allowing the running back to read the second level and choose his path based on the linebackers’ movement.

Price reads linebacker No. 14 coming downhill toward the line of scrimmage rather than flowing laterally, so he correctly decides to bounce the run outside. The biggest area for improvement is what happens next. You can see Price make two separate cuts, and on the second one he loses a little of his speed and explosiveness.

Again, this is not some glaring mistake, especially in a rookie’s first NFL game. With more experience, Price should become quicker with this read and get to the outside with one decisive cut rather than having to make two adjustments.

I may have missed one, but I believe this was Price’s only pass-blocking snap of the game. That’s probably a smart decision by Seattle. It’s not that Price is incapable of blocking, or unwilling to do it, but he is clearly inexperienced in pass protection and has shown both good and very poor reps in that area. He did catch two passes for six yards, but pass protection is something he’ll need to develop gradually. In the meantime, George Holani can continue to provide some of that experience in the backfield.

Nothing particularly flashy here, but the simple things are often underrated. The offensive line doesn’t create much separation, yet Price trusts the design, stays with his first read and, even with very little room to work with, lowers his pads and gets what he can.

Also, keep an eye on Anthony Bradford’s block on No. 24. It helps create just enough room for Price to finish the run.

One thing that stood out throughout Price’s tape is how disciplined he appears to be. He doesn’t seem overly eager to abandon the play design in search of something that isn’t there.

Seattle runs another outside-zone concept here. At one point, a gap appears between Abe Lucas and Anthony Bradford, but notice where Price’s eyes are. He doesn’t get sucked inside by the opening. Instead, he stays committed to working toward the edge. Once he turns the corner and gets going north, the explosiveness shows up again.

Being disciplined doesn’t mean lacking creativity.

Seattle runs another outside zone here, and this time the concept works particularly well. Price sticks with the initial track until he recognizes a better opportunity. Once he sees the lane inside, he makes the cut, turns upfield and takes on the defenders rather than trying to dance around contact. He eventually gets tackled, but there is plenty to like about the way he finishes the run and fights through contact.

This was one of the snaps that surprised me most in terms of Price’s speed. It’s another outside-zone run, and pay attention to how quickly Price gets moving before No. 24 can get to him. He manages to escape the tackle attempt and once again gets himself going north.

The officiating crew had already made several questionable decisions throughout the game, so perhaps they were trying to avoid adding another controversial call by not flagging JSN for a block in the back here.

Either way, once Price gets through it, you can see what his athleticism can bring to this offense. He appears to hit another gear once he gets north, and that acceleration is something worth watching as his role develops.

Bud Clark, Defensive Back — 0 snaps

Clark was one of the rookies I had the most confidence in coming into the season, so seeing him land on injured reserve was particularly disappointing.

There simply isn’t any defensive tape to evaluate yet, but his absence is significant when you consider the injuries Seattle has already dealt with in the secondary.

Julian Neal, Cornerback — 0 defensive snaps

With Seattle’s secondary dealing with multiple injuries, Neal could have had an opportunity to work his way into the defensive rotation.

Unfortunately, his injury during training camp significantly slowed his development. He saw only special-teams snaps in the opener, so there isn’t much to evaluate from a defensive standpoint yet.

Beau Stephens, Guard — 0 snaps

Stephens was inactive for the opener.

He showed some development during the final preseason game, but the fact that he was inactive suggests he still has some ground to make up on Seattle’s offensive line. At least for now, the coaching staff appears to have others names.

That’s notable considering Christian Haynes, the player Stephens was competing with in the preseason, had previously lost his starting opportunity to Sataoa Laumea — who is no longer even in the NFL.

For Stephens, the first step is simply getting active on game day.

Avery Smith, Cornerback — 0 defensive snaps

Because Smith is a rookie, even though he was not drafted or originally signed by Seattle, he’ll be included in this weekly rookie tracker.

Like Neal, Smith did not see any defensive snaps despite the injuries in Seattle’s secondary. His work came exclusively on special teams, so there isn’t much defensive tape to evaluate yet.

Final Thoughts

Unfortunately, this is pretty much what we expected before the season began.

The Seahawks 2026 rookie class was always likely to have a limited immediate impact, with Price being the one player most likely to contribute early. The injuries to Clark and Neal only make that reality more pronounced. That could remain the story for much of the season, although Neal or Smith could eventually find an opportunity if injuries create another opening in the secondary.

Stephens being inactive is also worth monitoring. In theory, it suggests that Grey Zabel and Anthony Bradford are healthy enough and playing well enough for Seattle to keep its current combination in place. For a team trying to stabilize the offensive line, that’s a positive development.

There are also a few rookies on the practice squad, although the path to playing time is considerably more difficult for most of them.

The two defensive backs would probably only be elevated to the active roster if injuries force Seattle’s hand and if Terrion Arnold and Trevon Diggs still “unavailable.” Emmanuel Henderson may be the one rookie on the practice squad with a realistic chance of seeing meaningful action this season at some point, while Deven Eastern looks more likely to spend the year developing and learning on the practice squad.

So, for now, Price is the rookie to watch.

And after his first 24 snaps, there are already enough flashes to make that worthwhile.

item.title: Javonte Williams really hurt the Cowboys on this play
item.description: Javonte Williams’ taunting penalty was inexcusable
item.content:encoded:
It appeared that the Dallas Cowboys were about to be down by seven points. As Javonte Williams was walking into the endzone after catching a pass from Dak Prescott, this was the collective thought.

Unfortunately, that thought was replaced by one of “what are you doing!?” as Williams was getting called for taunting in the process.

This was at a moment where the Cowboys were trying to rally. The score was leaving them only down by one possession. Ultimately the Cowboys were unable (shocker) to get a defensive stop so this wound up a moot point, but the player in question is a veteran, one who the Cowboys gave a second contract to, and had a completely avoidable mistake.

What’s more is that this happened on a team where the head coach, Brian Schottenheimer, preaches so much about culture. What kind of culture is it to make this kind of mistake? Why are you even taunting when you are still down by a touchdown?

Mistakes happen and people, hopefully, learn from them. This was a rough one for Javonte Williams.

item.title: The morning after: Aaron Rodgers needs more from his receivers
item.description: Aaron Rodgers’ box score doesn’t tell the story of how well he played in Week 1.
item.content:encoded:
Aaron Rodgers’ Week 1 box score does not do him justice in the slightest. The 42 year-old quarterback was slinging the pill all over the yard in the Pittsburgh Steelers’ 20-13 win to kickoff the season, but it was a victory that could have been much more convincing had Rodgers gotten help on some high-quality throws from his receivers.

Rodgers finished the day 24-of-40 for 221 yards and a touchdown. However, at least one other score was left off the board, and multiple big gains slipped through the hands of DK Metcalf.

The potential touchdown came when Rodgers launched a deep ball to Roman Wilson. Contact was made, but the third-year receiver fought through it, jumped in the air, and had the ball in his hands. When he came do the ground, the ball popped out, erasing what would have been a 44-yard score.

Metcalf had an especially forgetful day. On 10 targets, he totaled just four receptions for 40 yards. One was called back due to his second offensive pass interference of the day, erasing a 19-yard gain. Metcalf was also unable to drag his feet on a well-thrown Rodgers ball down the sideline that would have gone for 21, and he dropped Rodgers’ best throw of the day between two Falcons that would have gained 20.

In totality, those plays kept 104 yards and a touchdown off the board for Rodgers and the Steelers. Had those been caught, we’d be talking about a 28-of-40, 325 yard performance from the four-time MVP and a strong 27-point outing to begin his farewell season. Rodgers himself didn’t seem too bothered, though, as he noted explosive plays were there to be had.

“I think we did a lot of good things,” Rodgers told Pam Oliver after the game. “We had a chance to be really, really explosive. We had a couple drops, couple off-targets, couple non-calls that looked like penalties. So that changes the stats. We had a 40-yard PI that could have been a touchdown. We had a couple other ones that could have been big plays… it’s good to be out of here 1-0, though.”

The future Hall of Famer also made sure to praise his teammates, Cam Heyward and T.J. Watt, for their outstanding performances.

“T.J. played unbelievable,” Rodgers said. “He’s been on a different level this entire camp. I’m so proud of him [and] I love the way he leads. And Cam is the epitome of a Pittsburgh Steeler. To be able to share this team with them, to be able to share the leadership opportunity is really, really special in my last year and I’m just so thankful to just be back out here and play the game I love with guys I really respect and love as well.”

Rodgers and the Steelers will clearly be launching the ball more in 2026, which is a refreshing development. As is the group Rodgers calls “The old guys” continuing to halt time in its tracks. It’s the morning after game day, and we have much more to dive into.

Welcome back, T.J. Watt

We, and everyone else in the Steelers media space, have talked extensively about Watt’s performance, but with good reason. After two down seasons, the latter of which saw the three-time sack leader notch just seven takedowns of the quarterback after getting a massive pay day, many assumed we had seen the best of Watt. But maybe we had just seen the best of Watt in a Mike Tomlin-Teryl Austin defense.

The usage of the edge rushers has been a hot topic for years now. The lack of innovation and movement along the defensive line made Pittsburgh’s approach predictable. Plus, as Watt aged, his snap count stayed largely the same, naturally making him less explosive as games, and the season as a whole, went on.

On Sunday, Watt played 38 snaps – the fewest of Pittsburgh’s top three edge rushers. Mike McCarthy and Patrick Graham realize the fresher Watt stays through the game, the greater the chance for explosive plays. I’d say two sacks, three tackles for loss, and his first career pick-six is all the evidence we need that this scheme change, as well as a lower snap count, will reinvigorate the former Defensive Player of the Year and see him look more like the superstar we grew used to seeing week in and week out.

New Steelers defenders show up big

A pair of new Steelers defensive backs left their mark in their first action wearing Steelers colors. Pittsburgh native Jaquan Brisker picked off Cooper Rush to set up an Aaron Rodgers touchdown pass to Pat Freiermuth and finished the day with six tackles. Jamel Dean also had a nice outing, finishing with five tackles and a forced fumble on Bijan Robinson that killed a Falcons drive and forced a punt. Dean allowed just 31 yards through the air when targeted, and Brisker picked off the only pass that came his direction.

The Steelers allowed just four receptions to receivers all afternoon with only one of those receptions going for more than 20 yards. Yes, it came against Cooper Rush, but that’s how it is supposed to look when you face a bad quarterback. The secondary did its job and then some, even without Joey Porter Jr.

Quick-hitters

  • Michael Pittman had a quiet, but strong debut, catching all three passes thrown his way for 58 yards.
  • Talked about it yesterday, but Cam Heyward is ridiculous. Three pass deflections at the line of scrimmage. He is just seven shy of the NFL record for defensive linemen.
  • Max Iheanachor should start Week 2. Dylan Cook was bad, and the run game suffered in large part because of it.
  • Was good to see Pat Freiermuth start off on the right foot. He was vocal at the end of last season about the frustrations he had in seeing his snap count go way down. He handled it like a good teammate does, and is now back to being a top-notch pass-catching tight end.
  • Don’t let Alex Highsmith get lost in the shuffle. Due to Watt and Heyward’s big performances, you’d be forgiven if you forgot Highsmith had two sacks, as well.

Let us know what you think in the comments. Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more!
