item.title: Chiefs-Broncos: 5 things to watch in Week 1 matchup
item.description: Here are the things to keep a close eye on during Kansas City’s opening game.
item.content:encoded:
The Kansas City Chiefs will kick off the 2026 season at home against the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football.” The game will kick off at 7:15 Arrowhead time and air on ABC and ESPN.

This offseason, the Chiefs tried to reload after a disappointing 6-11 season in 2025, the first time Kansas City missed the playoffs since 2014. Multiple players will make regular-season debuts at Arrowhead on Monday Night.

Denver just had its best season in a decade, winning the AFC West and hosting the AFC Championship Game. After a decade of Kansas City dominance, the Broncos switched the script under head coach Sean Payton and finished 14-3, sweeping the Chiefs in the process.

Both teams have a lot to prove in 2026; one of football’s best stages will host the first AFC West battle of the season. Here are five things to watch:

1. The return of Patrick Mahomes

As improbable as it may seem, Chiefs star quarterback Patrick Mahomes will return to start his first game since December 14th of last season, when he tore his ACL in a loss to the Los Angeles Chargers.

For months, it has been widely speculated that Mahomes could miss time at the start of the 2026 season, but over the past couple of weeks, he and the Chiefs have made it clear he will suit up and start on Monday Night against Denver.

As a reminder, Mahomes did not play in any preseason games. It will be interesting to see how head coach Andy Reid and the offensive brain trust handle Mahomes early, especially against a fierce Denver defense.

It would be in the team’s best interest to give Mahomes as many layups as possible early in the game, allowing him to get into a flow as he readjusts to the speed of the game. I expect to see a few deep shots throughout the game.

2. How the Chiefs work around a hampered tackle position

The Josh Simmons saga continued and once again has taken a strange path with no clear answers. The only thing certain is that he will not play on Monday Night, as the Chiefs made clear.

Undrafted rookie Khalil Benson— who played mostly right tackle in camp— will make his first-ever NFL start in his first regular-season game. From starting in the National Championship for Indiana last season to making his NFL debut at left tackle, Benson has a tall task ahead of him.

Denver’s pass rush might not have the name power it did last season, but outside linebacker Nik Bonitto, 14 sacks in 2025, will still be screaming off the edge, and it would seem likely that they will line him up directly over Benson.

The Chiefs coaching staff should be prepared for this and able to provide slide protection to the left, as well as chips from tight ends and running backs.

While the move has some fans scratching their heads, having Benson start on the left side is an effort to keep Jaylon Moore on the right side of the line where he has appeared to be more comfortable, and where he will line up when Simmons returns from injury.

Moore needs to have a big game as the Chiefs will be giving help to Benson. I expect Reid to make the game plan very offensive-line friendly, with run-action looks as well as rollout plays.

3. New-look secondary

The Chiefs’ secondary looks much different than it did this time last year, but that is not necessarily a bad thing.

With Alohi Gilman and Jaden Hicks set to line up as the safeties — Chamarri Conner (Knee) will miss Week 1 — Nohl Williams, L’Jarius Sneed, and rookie Mansoor Delane will line up as the corners, with rookie Jadon Canady rotating in.

While the unit may take time to gel, it has the potential to become solid, especially under the tutelage of defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo and defensive backs Dave Merrit.

The unit will have its work cut out for it in Week 1 against a reloaded Broncos receiver unit featuring wide receivers Courtland Sutton, Jaylen Waddle, Marvin Mims and tight end Evan Engram.

As the unit gels, there could be some early issues, but the potential of the young corners, Delane and Williams, should help propel the unit into one of the stronger units in the NFL by the season’s end.

4. Rookie defensive linemen

Two of the Chiefs’ top 50 picks in the draft this past spring were defensive tackle Peter Woods and edge rusher R Mason Thomas.

Both flashed in training camp and the preseason, with Thomas drawing the most attention, displaying a combination of speed and bend that the Chiefs have not had off the edge in a while.

Woods was less disruptive in the preseason, but his impact should be more seen when he shares the field with star defensive tackle Chris Jones on Monday.

While both players excel in pass rushing situations, they will have to earn the right to get after Bo Nix. The Broncos have a powerful offensive line and good backs, which means the front seven, including both Thomas and Woods, will need to stand up against the run.

5. Kenneth Walker

It has been many years since the Chiefs have had a truly elite running back, but on Monday night, Kenneth Walker will make his debut with such a title.

The Chiefs didn’t use Walker much in the preseason, but with offensive line issues and Mahomes coming into his first game post-surgery, I would expect a heavy dose of the fifth-year running back.

Walker’s skill set to hit cutback lanes and explode out of the backfield in the passing game makes him a perfect fit for the Chiefs.

He is in for a big season.

item.title: New York Jets Week 1 Stock Up, Stock Down
item.description: Which Players Helped Their Stock Against The Titans?
item.content:encoded:
The season is finally here. And for a change, the Jets get a rare Week 1 win! The caveat, of course, is that the Titans are the Titans. But still, it’s nice to take the wins where you can get them. Who helped their stock, and who hurt it?

Let’s start with the stock ups.

Stock Up

Olu Fashanu

Now, I could mention the whole offensive line here, because I thought they were fantastic today. But I’ll mention Fashanu solely because, to me, he was the biggest X-factor for this team both this year and long-term.

Fashanu has proven to be an average NFL left tackle in his career thus far. But entering Year 3 at just 23 years old, the hope and expectation is that the former first-round pick will develop into an impact LT for years to come.

Today was a good start.

Against the Titans, Fashanu allowed just two pressures, no sacks, and graded out above 74.0 as both a pass blocker and run blocker. The whole offensive line played well, but Fashanu was extremely efficient against a talented Titans front.

This is exactly the type of performance the Jets need to see from him if he’s going to become the long-term answer at left tackle.

Azareye’h Thomas

I’ve recently said I’m kind of shocked about how little discussion Thomas has gotten surrounding the Jets this year. Cornerback is arguably the position where the Jets had the most question marks entering the season. Last year’s third-round pick quietly won the starting job opposite Brandon Stephens during training camp, and his first impression was quite good.

You didn’t hear his name too often, which is a good thing for a corner. But when you did, it was normally because of a positive play.

Thomas led the Jets in run stops with three, making a few terrific tackles on the perimeter, which was a huge weakness for this defense last year.

The competition wasn’t extremely good, but outside of a garbage-time touchdown he gave up, Thomas was excellent for the majority of the game. On a big third down, Ward challenged him down the field, and Thomas played fantastic coverage, using the sideline to his advantage to force an incompletion on Elic Ayomanor.

PFF agreed too with how Thomas performed, as he finished with an 80.3 overall grade and an 81.8 coverage grade.

At only 22 years old, Thomas turning into a sufficient starting boundary corner would be an excellent development for the Jets this year. Once again, the competition wasn’t great, but it’s a good start.

Kenyon Sadiq

Listen, Sadiq didn’t do anything incredible. But considering the injuries and all the negative vibes we heard about him this offseason, the fact that he was even a contributor at all is a positive to me for the rookie tight end in Week 1.

Sadiq only had three targets, but the fact that the Jets utilized more multi-tight end sets, something Frank Reich famously hasn’t done at his last two stops, makes me think there was at least some semblance of a plan for him.

There will be a lot more to watch for with Sadiq, but it’s very clear that he’s extremely athletic on the field. This isn’t just a guy who tested well athletically but doesn’t look the part in pads.

The touchdown wasn’t anything incredible, but it was a shrewd play call that used one of the Jets’ freak athletes to their advantage:

That’s exactly the type of thing I want to see from this offense. Find your good players and find creative ways to get them involved.

Geno Smith

The last person I’ll mention is Geno.

I don’t think it was all positive for Geno. In the first half, I saw some questionable clock management decisions, including a boneheaded checkdown that ended the Jets’ chances of getting points before halftime. He also seemed a bit too slow with his decision-making to start the game.

In the second half, though, I thought he was much, much better.

I don’t think he had to do anything crazy considering the game script, but he was fairly accurate and efficient and was able to push the ball downfield.

He ended with an 84.7 Total QBR, 0.26 EPA/play, and a 12.8 CPOE, all of which were elite numbers.

Now, I think the game script helped him heavily. And I’ve said all offseason that the main way to get competent play from Geno is to protect him.

The Jets showed a glimpse of what he can do when they do.

Stock Down

Now that we got the good out of the way, let’s get to the bad.

Fortunately, there wasn’t much of it.

Mason Taylor

Let’s just say this was a brutal game for Taylor.

And to be honest, he’s extremely fortunate it wasn’t worse.

Taylor was targeted three times and had an inexcusable drop that arguably could have been a fumble. It happened in a spot on the field where it could have been completely game-changing.

The other two targets resulted in catches, but one was a play that was doomed from the start, a tight end screen that went for negative yards and ultimately cost the Jets points.

I can’t hate on him too much for making that catch. That was more on Geno. But if you wanted to see some progress from the second-year tight end, this wasn’t a good start.

Arian Smith

Sticking with the theme of 2025 draft picks, my other big loser of the game was Arian Smith.

Again, I’ve long criticized the Smith pick. I don’t want to blame him for getting overdrafted. It was a boneheaded selection at the time.

But for a guy entering his second season, one where I thought he was lucky to make the roster in the first place, you cannot drop a routine catch on your only offensive snap of the game.

To me, it’s very clear where Smith will need to shift his focus if he wants to last in this league: special teams.

With his straight-line speed, he very much could end up being a positive contributor in that facet of the game.

We’ll see.

Overall

Overall, though, there were more highs than lows.

The Jets haven’t been over .500 in nearly two years. Let’s take the wins where we can get them.

The Titans might be really bad this year, but to be honest I don’t care. I’ll take it.

item.title: Fantasy Football Stock Report: Ashton Jeanty, Colston Loveland among notable risers, fallers in Week 1
item.description: Here are the players who helped and hurt their stock after Week 1 of fantasy football.
item.content:encoded:
As I write this on Sunday night, all but one Week 1 game is comfortably in the books, and as is always the case on opening weekend, we encountered a slew of surprises. Some promising, others concerning and many that may have affected our outlook on a player or an offense. We're all doing our best not to overreact to one Sunday (and one Wednesday and one Thursday), but some of these shifting perspectives are bound to have permanent ramifications.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Football league for the 2026 NFL season

With that in mind, I've compiled the (first) full weekly fantasy football stock report. These are the most notable risers and fallers heading into Week 2. 

STOCK UP

Ashton Jeanty, RB, Raiders

Ankle sprain, schmankle schprain (sorry, editors). Ashton Jeanty looked incredible on Sunday and had absolutely no limitations on his workload. He handled 23 carries and had six catches, totaling 147 yards while scoring twice through the air. He totaled 74 rushing yards after contact and scored both of his receiving touchdowns from the 13-yard line. Translation? The second-year RB's upside is arguably somewhere in the Christian McCaffrey stratosphere. The one caveat to all of this, of course, is that he did it against the Miami Dolphins. We'll see whether things change in Week 2 against the Chargers. But for now, Jeanty looks fully healthy and completely dominant, and anyone who got him at the "ankle sprain discount" is doing cartwheels.

Jalen Coker, WR, Panthers

At just 61% rostered on Yahoo, Jalen Coker was closer to being a waiver-wire player than a fantasy stud. Not anymore. The third-year wideout led the Panthers with nine targets, eight catches, 138 receiving yards and two touchdowns, finishing as the WR1 overall on Sunday (29.8 fantasy points). He ran the second-most routes on the team (32), behind Tetairoa McMillan (36), and averaged 13.8 air yards per target and 4.31 yards per route run. He made a very strong opening argument to be a 1B to McMillan's 1A this season. And while all of Carolina's numbers were inflated by this barn-burner of a game with Chicago, Coker had flashed late last year and looks like a legitimate third-year breakout candidate. He'll be among the most-added players on waivers this week (despite starting at 61%) and should be at least a FLEX consideration until further notice.

Chuba Hubbard, RB, Panthers

Elsewhere in this crazy Bears-Panthers game, Chuba Hubbard outsnapped Jonathon Brooks 41-to-13 and outcarried him 10-to-4. And while Brooks broke off a 48-yard reception, he was pretty silent as a rusher. Meanwhile, Hubbard racked up 49 yards on his 10 carries and scored from two yards out on the ground and four yards out through the air. Again, take it with a Chicago grain of salt. But at least for now, Hubbard is the lead back in Carolina and a borderline RB2 for fantasy.

David Montgomery, RB, Texans

This was somewhat predictable given how the Bills defense played the run last season (terribly), but David Montgomery's three touchdowns on Sunday were pretty encouraging. He only averaged 3.0 yards per carry on 20 totes and added 19 yards on three catches, but Montgomery scored rushing TDs from the goal line and the 18-yard line, and a receiving TD from the seven-yard line as well. If Houston is going to put him in position to score that often — and feed him more than 20 opportunities a game — Montgomery doesn't need to be that efficient to be effective for fantasy. He gets the Bengals next week as well, so expect another RB1-level outing from the artist formerly known as “Knuckles” (unless we're still calling him that).

Trevor Lawrence/Parker Washington, QB/WR, Jaguars

I promise, I was totally and completely normal about Parker Washington scoring the first touchdown of the Jaguars' 2026 season ... and ultimately putting up 16.8 fantasy points in the first half before essentially taking the rest of the game off in a blowout win. That's right, Washington logged all of his five catches for 83 yards by halftime, and then did not see a target the rest of the day. Jacksonville's not going to be up 24-0 after two quarters against most opponents — this was the Cleveland Browns after all — so we should get four quarters from Washington moving forward. He's a legitimate WR2 in fantasy (if not better).

Meanwhile, Trevor Lawrence has not just Washington, but also a resurgent Brian Thomas Jr., effective Jakobi Meyers, touchdown-scoring Brenton Strange and productive Bhayshul Tuten to throw to this season. He picked up right where he left off at the end of last season — scorching the league. Lawrence threw four touchdowns and posted a 150.6 passer rating ... and those four scores came on the team's first six drives before the aforementioned second-half coasting. At this rate, Lawrence could very well belong in the elite tier of fantasy QBs with Josh Allen and Lamar Jackson (and maybe Caleb Williams and Jaxson Dart, based on what we saw on Sunday).

Dallas Goedert, TE, Eagles

Had Dallas Goedert posted a decent day against the Commanders, I might have largely chalked it up to the Washington defense — which was, and clearly still is, terrible against tight ends. But the Eagles tight end was dominant, snagging a team-high four catches for a team-high 77 yards (on five targets) and scoring two touchdowns, including a 43-yarder late in the fourth quarter that essentially sealed the game for Philly. Dontayvion Wicks and DeVonta Smith were both good in their roles as well, but with A.J. Brown gone, Goedert looks like he's a focal point of this offense and probably the top red-zone threat (at least from outside the two-yard line). He was a fringe TE1 entering the year but could quickly cement himself near or inside the upper-tier at the position.

Isaiah Likely, TE, Giants

Speaking of tight ends taking their place in the elite ranks ... hello, Isaiah Likely. After being stuck behind Mark Andrews for years in Baltimore — and often flashing when given the chance — Likely followed John Harbaugh to New York. And boy did it work out (through one week). Likely was Jaxson Dart's best receiver, snagging all eight of his targets for 78 yards and two touchdowns, and making several critical plays in the eventual 28-20 win over the Cowboys on Sunday Night Football. He looked every bit the part of a true TE1 for both Big Blue and for fantasy. I'm not hesitating to put him right in the conversation with Colston Loveland (who we'll get to later), Tyler Warren and Tucker Kraft among the best tight ends not named Trey McBride (or Brock Bowers when healthy). It might sound like an overreaction, but what we saw on Sunday night makes too much sense to ignore. Likely to the moon.

DJ Moore, WR, Bills

Josh Allen's newest toy, DJ Moore, had an excellent first game with the Bills, catching five passes for 100 yards and a touchdown on eight targets. But even counting the 43-yard bomb that DJM caught for his score, this stat line doesn't tell the full story. Moore also drew an egregious pass interference penalty on a similar downfield pass earlier in the game, which would have resulted in a 47-yard touchdown without the penalty, and instead set up an Allen rushing TD from the one-yard line. Moore ran the most routes on the team and saw 19.4 air yards per target, ultimately accounting for 44% of the Bills' team air yards on the day. Also armed with Khalil Shakir underneath and Dalton Kincaid over the middle — not to mention James Cook II in the ground game — Allen and the Bills offense are poised for a best-ever type of season in 2026. It looks like Moore will thrive at the helm of the passing attack and is a strong WR2 with WR1 upside.

Christian Watson, WR, Packers

This is hard for me to admit as a long-time Christian Watson denier — and it was probably my worst "fade" of all-time — but the Packers wideout looked dominant on Sunday against what was one of the toughest defenses against wide receivers last year. He started things off with an 81-yard catch-and-run touchdown in the first quarter and proceeded to rack up 147 yards on six catches, with another TD from the two-yard line at the end of the first half. Watson currently sits just behind Coker for the highest fantasy score at the position (29.7 points). But most importantly, he saw eight targets. Watson had only seen eight or more targets five times prior in his career, and only caught six or more passes twice (both more than two years ago). He appears to be the true WR1 in Green Bay, and combining his efficiency with WR1 volume is a terrifying prospect. There's still a part of me that fears this receiving corps will be unpredictable week-to-week and Watson could be an afterthought next Sunday ... but that part is fading quickly.

STOCK DOWN

De'Von Achane, RB, Dolphins

We knew the Dolphins offense was going to be bad in 2026, and that De'Von Achane was a riskier early fantasy pick as a result. But Achane's unmatched big-play threat and elite receiving upside theoretically mitigated that risk. Welp. In a game Miami trailed throughout, against the Raiders no less, Achane had four receptions for 30 yards, which was nowhere near enough to offset just 36 rushing yards on 11 carries. Moreover, Miami did not have a single drive that finished inside the Raiders' 10-yard line ... and their only touchdown was a 13-yard rush vultured by Malik Willis. Achane will undoubtedly have some big games — perhaps even more often than not — but the floor being single-digit fantasy points in one of the few games all season the Dolphins weren't massive underdogs ... is discouraging.

Drake London/Kyle Pitts Sr., WR/TE, Falcons

There was some hope entering Week 1 that Cooper Rush might be a viable enough backup to support the top receiving options in Atlanta after Tua Tagovailoa's late injury scratch (and Michael Penix Jr. already out). Not so much. Rush completed just 12 passes against the Steelers ... and eight of those completions went to Bijan Robinson. No, I'm not joking. London and Pitts combined for two catches on five targets for 29 yards (and all the catches and yards were London's). We'll see how the quarterback situation shakes out next week and beyond — and both these players are too talented to be goose-egged or near goose-egged all year — but it's certainly not an encouraging start for players many had near the top of their positions in the preseason rankings.

Terry McLaurin, WR, Commanders

The good news is that this "fade" from my weekly column sort of balances out the Watson one ... I think? The bad news is that Terry McLaurin might be very hard to trust in fantasy this season. Washington's former WR1 — and yes, I mean that — saw just four targets and caught two for 14 yards. We were looking at a zero in his fantasy box score for the vast majority of the game, and it seemed extremely clear that Jayden Daniels and Co. preferred Stefon Diggs (who drew nine targets). Also, rookie Antonio Williams surged late in the game and might lay claim to a bigger piece of the pie moving forward. It might sound hyperbolically doom-and-gloom, but I was already very out on McLaurin this year and Week 1 was a near “nail-in-the-coffin.” He is no longer the clear No. 1 in the DMV, and I do not foresee a major bounce-back in 2026 after a very disappointing 2025. I'd honestly look to trade McLaurin to an optimistic buyer ASAP ... and might even consider Coker as the return.

Quinshon Judkins, RB, Browns

To put it unkindly, the Cleveland Browns are very, very bad, and that's very, very bad news for Quinshon Judkins. He was outrushed by Deshaun Watson on Sunday (on six fewer carries), finishing with just 33 yards on 12 totes (2.8 per carry) and adding two catches for 17 yards. The Browns didn't get into the red zone until late in the third quarter, and that drive ended in a field goal ... and was their only red-zone drive ending in points all day. And mind you, this dud of an opener for Judkins came with Dylan Sampson (knee) out for essentially the entire game. Working off Sunday's tape, it's hard to imagine a scenario where the Browns put together an effective offense at any point this season, which means Judkins will be incredibly hit-or-miss, based on big plays or occasional touchdowns. He was drafted as an RB2, but is already slipping into RB3 territory after that ineffective an opener.

Colston Loveland, TE, Bears

If you told me entering Week 1 that Colston Loveland would play the entire game, and that the Bears would score 59 points, but that the second-year tight end would finish with zero, zilch, nada ... I would have chuckled and checked your temperature. Unfortunately, that's exactly what happened. It was borderline inexplicable, especially considering Loveland ran the most routes on the team (32) and Cole Kmet had two catches for 35 yards and a touchdown. Honestly, I expect a significant rebound from Loveland moving forward — he's too talented, and Kalif Raymond is unlikely to see nine targets again — but we should not see goose eggs in 59-burgers from our elite fantasy tight ends. Loveland is on “Concern Watch” for the next couple weeks.

item.title: AFC North: 3 winners, but who looked good, who had injuries, and who is suspect?
item.description: The AFC North saw the Cleveland Browns as the only losers, but how did the Steelers, Bengals, and Ravens actually look?
item.content:encoded:
As Cleveland Browns fans lament another terrible start to an NFL season, the beat goes on around the AFC North. The Browns are the lone team to lose in Week 1, a drubbing handed to them by the Jacksonville Jaguars, with many turning their attention to the 2027 NFL draft to try to avoid thinking about what former Cleveland QB Baker Mayfield might do in Week 2.

As always, we still want to keep track of what is going on in the AFC North, including two big contract issues that could lead to rumors and a trade.

Baker hands Bengals the game

It is almost impossible to have an honest, good conversation about Baker Mayfield around Cleveland fans. For a lot of good reasons, as mentioned in The Feed. Those convesations, however, will probably never stop especially with Week 2’s matchup.

In Week 1, the Cincinnati Bengals once again saw the full Baker experience. Mayfield completed 23 of 28 passes for 216 with zero touchdowns and zero interceptions. He willed the team back into the game, including five carries for 30 yards and a touchdown, while handing, almost quite literally, the game to the Bengals with three fumbles.

For Cincinnati, the defense was much improved while the offense was good, not great, as they get ramped up. No one had two catches for 12 yards for Ja’Marr Chase also leading to a Bengals victory, but he we are.

Steelers hold off Kevin Stefanski, 3rd-string QB

Not sure what Stefanski did in a past life, but his quarterback options have been limited for quite a few years. On Sunday, that included starting third-stringer Cooper Rush, who completed just 12 of 22 passes for 143 yards, one touchdown, and two interceptions, including a back-breaking pick-6.

Pittsburgh’s offense did just enough, and the defense was solid. The opponent drops the excitement level for Steelers fans, although a victory is a victory.

Ravens control the game, have injury concerns coming out

With four straight touchdowns between the first and second quarter, the Baltimore Ravens were in control 28-6, then 31-13 heading into halftime. While the Bengals and Steelers didn’t have huge offensive days, the Ravens saw Lamar Jackson throw for 324 yards, Derrick Henry rush for 144 yards, and Zay Flowers have 150 yards receiving.

The bad news for Baltimore is Flowers’ hamstring issue popped up, which isn’t expected to be long-term but is notable for a speedster. On top of that, hotshot rookie Jakobi Lane has a fractured wrist and could miss signficant time.

Overall, the Ravens looked the most dominant of the three winning AFC North teams in Week 1.

item.title: Broncos get huge injury news ahead of Week 3 showdown with Rams
item.description: The Rams placed star pass rusher Myles Garrett on the IR and he will miss the Week 3 matchup vs. the Broncos
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles had a ton of hype entering the 2026 season. They acquired star pass rusher Myles Garrett from the Cleveland Browns, traded for star cornerback Trent McDuffie from the Chiefs, and coaxed star pass rusher Aaron Donald out of retirement to join their defense. They had a loaded roster on paper and were ready to dominate their already banged-up divisional rivals the San Francisco 49ers in Australia on primetime with the game being aired on Netflix.

Well, that did not happen.

Not only did the Rams lose, they were dominated, jet lagged, and blown out by their divisional rivals. The news did not get better for them this weekend. On Sunday, it was reported by NFL Network’s lead league insider Ian Rapoport that star pass rusher Myles Garrett is set to undergo knee surgery and is headed to the injured reserve. This means that Garrett will miss a minimum of 4 games which includes a primetime matchup vs. the Denver Broncos in Week 3.

This is a huge loss for the Rams and a big break for the Broncos and the rest of the teams playing the Rams while Garrett is sidelined. Now, the Rams will be getting back Aaron Donald, but the 35-year old who has sat out the past two seasons will likely still be on a snap count and shaking off some rust during their Week 3 matchup vs. the Broncos.

The Broncos have one of the best offensive lines in the NFL (If not the best), and this was set to be a fun strength vs. strength matchup. However, with Garrett sidelined, the Broncos will now have the edge against a still talented Rams front 7.

Before we worry about Week 3, the Broncos have to take care of business tonight vs. their Divisional Rivals, the Kansas City Chiefs. They will be playing on the road in loud Arrowhead and will be dealing with the return of quarterback Patrick Mahomes who is returning from a major knee injury. Then, in Week 2, they will be hosting the Jacksonville Jaguars, who were the only team last season to really beat the Broncos. The rest of their losses were one-score games with penalities, missed opportunities, and injuries being a big reason why they lost. That wasn’t the case vs. the Jaguars. They dominated the Broncos late last season, and now Bo Nix and the Broncos will seek revenge against their small market rivals.

Injuries happen and reshape the landscape of the NFL and the Broncos schedule each and every week, and the loss of Myles Garrett is a big one for the Rams. The Broncos will catch a break there but first, will need to take care of business against the Chiefs and Jaguars before they can focus on the Garrett-less Rams squad.

item.title: Badgers snap counts, grades on defense vs. Western Illinois: Who played well and who struggled?
item.description: The Badgers saw some flourish, while others had up and down games in Week 2.
item.content:encoded:
The Wisconsin Badgers comfortably beat the Western Illinois Leathernecks on Saturday, but the score didn’t capture the full picture, as it was an up-and-down game for the home team at Camp Randall Stadium.

There were a lot of questions about the defense for Wisconsin, as they struggled to contain the run at times against a team that lost 41-10 to Illinois State the week before.

Here are the snap counts and PFF grades for every player on defense for the Badgers against Western Illinois.

Defensive Line

item.title: Packers Discussion: 1st impressions of Jonathan Gannon’s defense
item.description: What did you think of Jonathan Gannon’s debut?
item.content:encoded:
I’m sure that we’re going to talk about the offensive line a lot this week, so I just want to give this space for people to fire off their thoughts on another major subject: the first game that Jonathan Gannon called on the defensive side of the ball. For the most part, I thought the defense did fine on Sunday.

The defense gave up 3.1 yards per attempt in the run game and 4.9 yards per dropback. It’s amazing how the Minnesota Vikings were able to get 39 points with those numbers. They scored 29 points straight with only one drive over 28 yards, because the offense not only was getting off the field quickly but also giving the defense short fields to defend.

What really hurt Green Bay at the end was that Carrington Valentine was playing snaps at cornerback, as he was run at directly for a touchdown and gave up another score to Justin Jefferson on a catch-and-run opportunity.

In general, the Packers pretty much played their base 3-4 defense and nickel defenses, as the Penny defense was sort of shelved. I thought Gannon put Lukas Van Ness and Edgerrin Cooper in really good positions to succeed, leading to some of their best games as pros. Keisean Nixon had a good game, too. Zaire Franklin didn’t get exposed in coverage, outside of the touchdown where he was the runner in Tampa 2 (a changeup play that Green Bay just got caught in).

item.title: Lions vs. Saints snap counts: Several defensive rotations unveiled
item.description: Exploring how and why the Lions used their personnel in Week 1 vs. Saints.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions needed overtime to secure a 31-30 win over the New Orleans Saints in Week 1, but a win is a win in September as teams adjust to a new season. Let’s look at the snap counts from this game and see what they mean for the depth chart hierarchy and what we can glean moving forward.

Quarterback

  • Jared Goff: 77 snaps (100%)
  • Josh Dobbs: Did not play (DNP)

With the Lions’ run game clicking, Goff had an average day at the office on Sunday, though the Saints’ fast tempo sped up the game and created more opportunities for both offenses.

Running back

  • Jahmyr Gibbs: 57 (74%)
  • Sione Vaki: 22 (29%) — 24 special teams (71%)
  • Jacob Saylors: 0 (0%) — 24 (71%)

We were told Gibbs would be the workhorse back, and he certainly was in the opener, carrying the ball a league-leading 29 times and rushing for a league-leading 156 yards. He also added five receptions for another 30 yards for good measure. Despite Gibbs touching the ball a ton, he was still on the field only 74% of the time, leaving 20 opportunities for Vaki and two snaps when they were on the field simultaneously.

It was an up-and-down day for Vaki’s first run as RB2, showing well in pass protection and as a receiver, but in the locker room after the game, he was left frustrated with the mistakes he made. When I asked him to point out the parts of his game he was happy with, he had this to say:

“To be honest, I couldn’t tell you. I feel like there’s nothing but improvement that needs to happen.”

It’s worth noting that, according to PFF, 20 of Vaki’s 22 reps came on passing downs, which points to coaches’ confidence in his ability to hold up in one of the more critical components of a running back’s responsibilities.

Wide receiver

  • Amon-Ra St. Brown: 69 (90%)
  • Jameson Williams: 65 (84%)
  • Isaac TeSlaa: 52 (68%)
  • Tay Martin: 0 (0%) — 24 (71%)
  • Tom Kennedy: 0 (0%) — 11 (32%)

The Lions rolled with just three receivers on offense, with Martin and Kennedy taking on starting roles on special teams. Martin was fantastic as a gunner on punts and on kickoff coverage, securing a career-high three special teams tackles.

“I just wanted to make sure I made Dan (Campbell) right for believing in me,” Martin said of using special teams to make the active roster. “I’ve been waiting on this chance my whole life, to go out there on the 53-man roster and make some plays.”

Tight end

  • Sam LaPorta: 62 (81%)
  • Brock Wright: 39 (51%) — 11 (32%)
  • Tyler Conklin: 10 (13%)
  • Jackson Meeks: 0 (0%) — 18 (53%)

No real surprises here, as the Lions were expected to utilize all three of their top tight ends, and the distribution of snaps is very similar to what we’ve seen in previous years.

Offensive line

  • LT Penei Sewell: 77 (100%) — 5 (15%)
  • C Juice Scruggs: 77 (100%) — 5 (15%)
  • RG Tate Ratledge: 77 (100%) — 5 (15%)
  • RT Blake Miller: 77 (100%) — 5 (15%)
  • G Ben Bartch: 66 (86%) — 5 (15%)
  • LG Christian Mahogany: 11 (14%)
  • OT Larry Borom: 9 (12%) — 5 (15%)
  • G/T Miles Frazier: 0 (0%) — 5 (15%)

Mahogany got the start, but an awkward injury on the 11th offensive play cost him the rest of the game. The initial scan of his knee was negative, and Mahogany was in good spirits in the locker room, suggesting it’s not a long-term injury, but on a short week, the Lions may continue to lean on Bartch to start at left guard.

Borom found the field nine times in Jumbo sets, and offensive coordinator Drew Petzing was very creative in his usage, lining him up as a tight end and at left tackle. That gave the Lions the opportunity to move Sewell all over the formation, create mismatches in the run game, and was a catalyst in both of Gibbs’ rushing touchdowns.

Interior defensive line

  • 3T Alim McNeill: 83 (92%) — 5 (15%)
  • 3T Skyler Gill-Howard: 47 (52%) — 5 (15%)
  • DT Tyleik Williams: 35 (39%) — 5 (15%)
  • DL Ben Stille: 9 (10%)
  • 3T Mekhi Wingo — INACTIVE

McNeill seeing the field on 92% of defensive snaps is borderline insane for a big man. So why do it? His positional versatility and ability to impact the game from multiple spots is a massive advantage for defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard.

With the Lions maintaining a double-digit lead for most of the game, the Saints threw the ball often. That situation led the Lions to lean on rookie Gill-Howard more than starter Williams. After the game, he talked with Pride of Detroit about his impact on the game:

“I think I need to pass rush way better. There were times when I was rushing too down the middle, or I got stuck in a gap—I had a few decent rushes for sure, but I felt like the area I took a step (forward) was in the run game. I didn’t get moved (off the ball) at all.”

Gill-Howard’s assessment is backed up by PFF, who assigned him a 76.8 grade for his run defense, the second-highest on the team in Week 1.

EDGE

  • EDGE Aidan Hutchinson: 75 (83%)
  • Rush End DJ Wonnum: 69 (77%) — 5 (15%)
  • EDGE Derrick Moore: 18 (20%)
  • Big End Tyler Lacy: 15 (17%)
  • Rush End Eric O’Neill: 4 (4%) — 17 (50%)
  • Big End Ahmed Hassanein — INACTIVE

Like McNeill, Hutchinson played a ridiculous amount of snaps in this game, but it was surely hard to take him off the field when he was so dominant. Not only did Hutchinson secure two sacks, but he leads the NFL in pressures in both PFF (10) and NFL Pro’s (10) metrics.

With the Lions electing to play more nickel defense in this game, that meant more Wonnum, and he rewarded Sheppard with his performance, forcing six pressures (tied for seventh best in the NFL, per NFL Pro) and a couple of pass breakups at the line of scrimmage.

O’Neill, who was active over Hassanein, showed why with his special teams performance, securing two special teams tackles at critical moments.

Linebacker

  • MIKE Jack Campbell: 90 (100%) — 5 (15%)
  • SAM Derrick Barnes: 77 (86%) — 13 (38%)
  • WILL Malcolm Rodriguez: 20 (22%) — 19 (56%)
  • WILL Devin White: 18 (20%)
  • SAM Trevor Nowaske: 8 (9%) — 29 (85%)
  • MIKE Joe Bachie: 0 (0%) — 18 (53%)
  • MIKE Jimmy Rolder — INACTIVE

While Campbell played every down on defense, the rest of the linebackers were used more situationally, with Barnes getting the most opportunities because of his versatility—and he didn’t disappoint. Barnes secured an interception, was credited with three run stops and two pressures (per PFF), while also adding a sack for good measure.

Rodriguez and White split WILL linebacker duties, each finding the field in situation-specific roles. Nowaske came on for more bulk at the line of scrimmage, while Bachie was relegated to special teams.

Cornerback

  • CB D.J. Reed: 89 (99%)
  • CB Rock Ya-Sin: 89 (99%) — 5 (15%)
  • NB/CB Roger McCreary: 39 (43%) — 16 (47%)
  • NB Keith Abney: 25 (28%) — 5 (15%)
  • CB Khalil Dorsey: 0 (0%) — 23 (68%)
  • CB Ennis Rakestraw — INACTIVE

Reed and Ya-Sin only missed one rep each on a grueling 90-play afternoon, while McCreary took over the Christian Izien every-down role in the slot with Abney backing him up in obvious passing situations. Overall, the Lions played nickel roughly 70% of defensive downs, and while some of that was adjusting to the Saints throwing the ball, it also reflects what we have seen in training camp.

Safety

  • S Avonte Maddox: 85 (94%)
  • S Thomas Harper: 54 (60%) — 17 (50%)
  • S Chuck Clark: 41 (46%) — 5 (15%)
  • NB/S Christian Izien — INACTIVE

One of the interesting wrinkles to come out of this game is how the Lions utilized their safeties. While Maddox and Clark were the clear starters all training camp, coaches alluded to Harper increasing his role and competing for starter-level snaps. We saw Harper start the majority of the time the Lions were in nickel, while Clark appeared to be the preferred option in the Lions’ base defense. This approach looked effective, as each allowed only one reception on two targets, while Clark also secured an interception. Look for the Lions to continue rotating their safeties moving forward.

Specialists

  • P Jack Fox: 12 (35%)
  • LS Hogan Hatten: 12 (35%)
  • K Jake Bates: 11 (32%)

Outside of Martin and O’Neill looking sharp in kick/punt coverage, the special teams as a whole looked rusty. Bates mishit kicks on kickoffs, while Fox unexpectedly shorted a few of his punts. Nothing was detrimental overall, but there are certainly things to clean up.

item.title: Mike Tomlin offers theory to explain Week 1's record-breaking offensive explosion across the NFL
item.description: Per multiple metrics, Sunday's Week 1 slate and the entire set of games leading up to Sunday night were historic in terms of scoring.
item.content:encoded:
If you thought Week 1 in the NFL was explosive, you thought right.

Per multiple metrics, Sunday's Week 1 slate and the entire set of games leading up to Sunday night were historic in terms of scoring.

Entering "Monday Night Football" between the Kansas City Chiefs and Denver Broncos, Week 1 was the highest scoring in the NFL since the 1970 AFL-NFL merger by average with 50.0 combined points per game.

This is the highest scoring Week 1 since the 1970 NFL-AFL merger, though there are still two games to go pic.twitter.com/nrI0KsJvFw

— Ben Volin (@BenVolin) September 13, 2026

Per NBC, Sunday's slate alone marked the highest-scoring Week 1 Sunday since the merger.

Leading the way was the barn-burner between the Bears and Panthers in which Chicago secured a 59-37 win over Carolina in Charlotte. That matchup set the single-game scoring record for a Week 1 game when Chicago held a 52-37 lead with 4:00 remaining. Chicago's final touchdown was just gravy.

Mike Tomlin explains his theory on offensive explosion

So what's the reason behind the offensive explosion? Mike Tomlin has a theory.

The recently retired Pittsburgh Steelers head coach continues to shine in his new role as an analyst for NBC's game broadcasts. He offered his reasoning for the offensive fireworks during halftime of Sunday night's matchup between the Dallas Cowboys and New York Giants.

"I think how we practice and how we prepare our teams today really kind of lends itself to offenses starting faster than they have historically," Tomlin told host Maria Taylor. "What I mean by that is there is less violence in team development. There are less padded practices. Even the drills that they do are more geared to skill development — 7 on 7 and things of that nature.

"Defenses spend less time shedding blocks and tackling than they used to 25 years ago when I came into the league."

Does Tomlin's theory hold water?

That seems a reasonable theory. And it's based on Tomlin's first-hand experience as an NFL head coach, coordinator and assistant for 25 seasons before this one.

Tomlin's theory suggests that scoring will go down. Per Tomlin, defenses aren't as prepared for Week 1 as offenses. But with each week of game experience and regular-season practice, defensive players and units will hone their craft, physicality and skills, and, theoretically, even the playing field with their offensive counterparts.

Only time will tell if that theory holds up. But until proven otherwise, it suggests that we should continue to anticipate high-scoring games early in the season.

item.title: A.J. Brown reportedly expected to miss more than 4 games on injured reserve
item.description: The Patriots wide receiver hurt his ankle last Wednesday and has since been placed on injured reserve.
item.content:encoded:
The New England Patriots did not just lose their season opener against the Seattle Seahawks last Wednesday, they also lost wide receiver A.J. Brown to injury. The high-prized offseason trade acquisition suffered a high-ankle sprain and was since placed on injured reserve.

While that means he will miss at least four games, the expectation is that his absence will be longer than that.

“My understanding is the expectation is he misses six weeks,” NFL Network insider Rapoport said on the air on Sunday. “Generally, it is four to six. This is a little more serious. Six weeks, no surgery planned.”

Brown caught three passes for 26 yards in his Patriots debut, but hurt his ankle in the early third quarter while diving for an under-thrown Drake Maye third-down pass. He remained on the ground before gingerly walking to the blue medical tent on the sidelines; he subsequently reemerged and headed to the locker room for further testing, where he was then ruled out for the remainder of the game.

The Patriots did score three more points with Brown sidelined, to cap the very series he departed with a 50-yard Andy Borregales field goal. Afterward, however, the team was shut out and ended up losing 13-10.

Now on injured reserve, Brown will not be available against the Steelers, Jaguars and Bills. If indeed held out for six weeks, he would also miss games against the Raiders and Jets. In his place, the Patriots’ outside wide receiver group will be headed by Romeo Doubs, Mack Hollins and Kyle Williams.

The group will see its first extended action without Brown on Sunday against Pittsburgh. Kickoff for the Patriots’ home opener at Gillette Stadium is scheduled for 1 p.m. ET.

item.title: NFL Week 2 odds: Eagles open as big road favorites against Titans
item.description: Are you betting on the Birds?
item.content:encoded:
The way I’d frame the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 1 win over the Washington Commanders? I’d say it’s a performance to build on.

The offense as a collective clearly needs to be better. They only managed 10 first downs on Sunday … the fewest of any team in the league so far.

Maybe Sean Mannion’s group can get it going against the Tennessee Titans? The Eagles are entering Week 2 as seven-point road favorites, according to FanDuel.

This after the Titans, now coached by Robert Saleh, lost to the New York Jets by a final score of 23 to 10. Geno Smith completed 19 of 24 attempts for 215 yards and a 104 passer rating. The Jets’ top two running backs combined for 142 rushing yards and one touchdown on 32 carries (4.4 average).

Until we actually see the Eagles prove they can block better, it might be hard to fully believe it. But you have to feel good about Jalen Hurts’ ability to make plays for this team after watching what he did against the Commanders. You also have to like Vic Fangio’s chances of being able to stifle the Titans’ offense, which managed a mere 195 yards yesterday. That’s 123 fewer yards than the Eagles managed to muster in Week 1.

The Titans will be motivated to avoid two straight home losses to start the 2026 season but I believe in the Birds to emerge victorious. Will they definitely cover? I’ll lean yes, though I can’t say I’m 100% confident.

What say you?

item.title: Vikes Views: Sunday King – Packers at Vikings
item.description: Man I love when they beat the Packers. The Minnesota Vikings gave us a scare with the slow start to the game. That sinking feeling was helped along with the nasty hit that knocked out Kyler Murray for the game, and likely the next one. However, the team showed resilience and climbed back into the […]
item.content:encoded:
Man I love when they beat the Packers. The Minnesota Vikings gave us a scare with the slow start to the game. That sinking feeling was helped along with the nasty hit that knocked out Kyler Murray for the game, and likely the next one. However, the team showed resilience and climbed back into the game. The closing quarter was a defensive masterpiece from Brian Flores. This team has some gumption.

Kevin O’Connell

This team could’ve easily fallen apart to boos at home. KOC has shown his system can work with just about anyone at QB. He once again maintained his composure after losing his starting QB. The offense ended the game with four straight touchdowns, granted only one drive was more than 30 yards. Finishing in the Red Zone and winning the turnover battle decided the game. KOC’s offense was efficient when opportunities presented themselves. The Vikings consistently finished drives with touchdowns instead of settling for field goals.

Brian Flores

You can’t mention the coaching staff without talking about Brian Flores. It was a rough start with the Packers starting the game with three straight scoring drives and a touchdown to end the first half. The Vikings defense settled down and only allowed three points in the 2nd half. The 4th quarter drive list for the Packers was Turnover on Downs, Fumble, Interception, Turnover on Downs. The defense handed the offense possessions at the Packers’ 1-yard line and 14-yard line. The inventive pressures were too much for the Packers’ OL and Jordan Love. It was as dominant as you’ll ever see a defense play a quarter.

Carson Wentz

It’s not easy to maintain focus around the constant attention JJ McCarthy and Kyler Murray received this offseason. Wentz put in the work and got ready to play, despite the distractions. He didn’t put up a ton of yards, mainly because he didn’t have to. Wentz wisely leaned on veterans Justin Jefferson and TJ Hockenson. Quick, efficient and professional game from Carson Wentz.

Justin Jefferson

It’s painfully obvious Jefferson was the only real weapon the Vikings had on Sunday. He caught just about everything that was thrown his way. Jefferson comes to play every Sunday and doesn’t complain about the constant QB carousel. He’s on this list almost every week and it’d be hard to justify leaving him off this week.

Myles Price

Price looked dangerous every time he returned a kick. There were a couple of shoe-string tackles that saved the Packers earlier in the game. His 61-yard return in the 3rd quarter started the comeback. It was a huge momentum swing, and the offense was able to take advantage. You never know where the spark might come from, and price took advantage of the little bit of opportunity he was given.

Honorable Mentions:

Will Reichard – perfect as usual, is he already the GOAT Vikings kicker?

Andrew Van Ginkel – a lot of the defensive guys could be listed, but he had the fumble recovery on Love in the 4th quarter.

Harrison Smith – just glad he’s playing again.

item.title: Eagles rookie report card: Need more from Makai Lemon
item.description: Keeping an eye on Philadelphia’s 2026 NFL Draft picks.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles pieced together a divisional win over the Washington Commadners on Sunday, showing exciting flashes on both sides of the ball as they shook some rust off. While there is much to be encouraged about, the Eagles’ rookies are not among those reasons for optimism. Here are the big takeaways from Philadelphia’s 2026 NFL Draft class in Week 1. 

Makai Lemon: D

It was to be expected that Makai Lemon would have a slow start to the season given his lack of participation in the offseason. He missed a lot of practice time due to his hamstring injury. But Sunday was still rough. Lemon was targeted four times, catching three passes and finishing the day with negative five yards. That is really tough, but it’s not all on him. 

Lemon’s usage was odd to say the least. Sean Mannion and company are still clearly trying to get a handle on what to do with this receiving group after DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks. Two of Lemon’s catches were on doomed screens and one was a short perimeter target. Given what Lemon was good at, I think he should live in the slot and eat up short targets there to get him going. 

Sunday was not his day, but it’s obvious the team wants him out there given 29 receiver snaps, which was the third-most at his position. Hopefully, going forward the Eagles find different ways to get Lemon involved as he gets more comfortable with the playbook. 

Other Observations

  • Eli Stowers was placed on injured reserve as the Eagles put him on the backburner. That’s a bummer and I hope he can figure it out at some point this season. The good news for the Eagles is that Dallas Goedert looks awesome. Throwback to the Eagles drafting Goedert in the second round of the 2018 NFL Draft and then Zach Ertz immediately having the best season of his career. 
  • Rookie blockers Markel Bell and Micah Morris are beginning this season as depth players; the former was active while the latter was a healthy scratch. That being said, Landon Dickerson looked rough yesterday. Hopefully it is just a one-off bad day for the three-time Pro Bowler, but he really didn’t look like himself. That is worth monitoring, and luckily the Eagles have the depth to fill in if Dickerson can’t go. 
  • Cole Payton was predictably inactive as QB4. No special teams role for him.

item.title: Position grades from the Patriots’ loss to the Seahawks
item.description: Grading each Patriots position group after their 13-10 loss against the Seahawks.
item.content:encoded:
The New England Patriots started their 2026 season the way they ended their 2025 campaign, with a loss to the Seattle Seahawks. The 13-10 game was as tightly-contested as the final score indicated, meaning that the visiting Patriots were not as bad as their minus-3 turnover differential or current 0-1 record would suggest.

We already spoke about the standout performances from the game. Now, after rewatching it through broadcast copy and coach’s film, here are our final position grades from the Patriots’ defeat.

Patriots position grades from NFL Week 1

Quarterback: For three quarters, Drake Maye played the game he needed to play for the Patriots to win. He took what the defense gave him, showed good accuracy in the short and intermediate parts of the field, and most importantly did not make any back-breaking mistakes. Then came the fourth quarter and a dramatic flipping of the switch. The patience he showed earlier disappeared as he launched a deep ball toward a double-covered Romeo Doubs that ended up as the first of three interceptions. That pick was a turning point for New England and its young QB, who still made some positive plays but ultimately crumbled while trying his version of “hero ball.” | Grade: D+

Running back: No TreVeyon Henderson meant a heavy workload for Rhamondre Stevenson, and he did what he could. Ultimately, however, he found little room to run en route to gaining just 51 yards on 18 carries for an underwhelming 2.8-yard average. He was more effective as a receiver, finishing with 44 yards on five catches, but did give up one hit against Drake Maye. The only other backs to see action — Corey Kiner and Lan Larison — combined to play 11 snaps, with the former carrying the ball six times for 11 yards and the latter working exclusively as a receiver and gaining 9 yards on a pair of receptions. | Grade: B-

Wide receiver: The Patriots’ new-look receiver group had a challenging first day. A.J. Brown was lost to a high-ankle sprain after catching three passes for 26 yards, while fellow offseason pickup Romeo Doubs was held without a reception on three targets — one of them an interception, the other a rough drop. The player most consistently open against the Seahawks was DeMario Douglas, who finished with five catches for 20 yards. Mack Hollins was a go-to-guy for Drake Maye on the final drive and actually finished the game with a team-high 51 receiving yards. He also was involved on the game-losing interception, failing to properly clean out space underneath for Hunter Henry. Kyle Williams was largely a non-factor even after Brown departed in the early second half. | Grade: C-

Tight end: It was a mixed bag for New England’s tight ends, only two of whom actually saw the field on offense. Hunter Henry caught all three of his passes for 26 combined yards, but also did not come off the line quickly enough on the final Drake Maye interception. Eli Raridon, meanwhile, caught the first touchdown of the season and threw a key block on Rhamondre Stevenson’s longest run of the day, a 12-yarder on the final drive. However, he also was responsible for two stuffed runs. | Grade: B

Offensive line: No statistic from Wednesday’s game might be as damning for the offensive line as this one: Rhamondre Stevenson and Corey Kiner combined to gain 62 yards on the ground, with 59 of those coming after contact. Frankly, the running game had almost no room to operate, and looked the part. To the line’s credit, though, it did show some improvement in pass protection since the Super Bowl. However, Drake Maye was still pressured on 38.1% of his dropbacks even though he ended up taking just three sacks. As for individual efforts, Alijah Vera-Tucker had a rough Patriots debut, while Jared Wilson — who hurt his hand in the early second half — also struggled with consistency. Will Campbell, meanwhile, looked good outside of two penalties. | Grade: C–

Defensive line: The Seahawks found some room to run early on and ended up with 97 yards on 22 carries, an average of 4.4 yards per attempt. Still, there were some solid moments both inside — such as Milton Williams’ 3rd-and-1 stuff in the fourth quarter — and on the edge. The latter was particularly encouraging after it was a major concern during joint practices with the Colts and Eagles. The pass rush from that part of the line was somewhat inconsistent outside of Dre’Mont Jones, with both of the group’s sacks of the clean-up variety. Inside, Christian Barmore gave Seattle’s interior line all it could handle even though his pressure total (4) does not quite reflect his impact. | Grade: B–

Linebacker: Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss were the only off-ball linebackers to play on the defensive side of the ball. They were unsurprisingly actively involved, registering a combined 12 tackles but also missing three takedown attempts. Spillane also struggled to run with quarterback Drew Lock on one outside scramble. All in all, they had an adequate debut but were unable to provide any impact plays from the second level. | Grade: C

Cornerback: Christian Gonzalez posted a shutout in 10 coverage matchups with Jaxon Smith-Njigba and looked every bit like the highest-paid cornerback in football he is. He did drop an interception and appeared a bit overeager on a run blitz on what ultimately ended as a 45-yard catch-and-run touchdown from the NFL Offensive Player of the Year, but overall looked like the shutdown cornerback is being paid to be. The other cornerbacks, meanwhile, performed at a high level as well. The only real blemish was Marcus Jones giving up a 24-yard catch to convert a third down before the Seahawks’ first field goal, but even that play was more due to Cooper Kupp’s concentration and ball skills rather than some bad coverage. | Grade: B+

Safety: Craig Woodson had one of the best games of his young career against the Seahawks in the Super Bowl, but was less effective in the rematch on Wednesday. He missed a pair of tackles, including when he came in too hot on Jaxon Smith-Njiba’s long touchdown, and would have given up a touchdown to Cooper Kupp if not for an unrelated offensive infraction. Kevin Byard was solid in his Patriots debut, while the heavily-involved Dell Pettus had an up-and-down day as well. | Grade: C–

Special teams: New England’s kicking game operation performed well. Andy Borregales made his lone field goal try from 50 yards out and split the uprights on an extra point. New punter Mitch Wishnowsky averaged 44.3 yards on four kicks, and pinned Seattle inside the 20 on three of them. Rashid Shaheed did have one 30-yard kickoff return but otherwise was held in check. Meanwhile, Kyle Williams averaged a solid 29.0 yards per kickoff return. Marcus Jones, on the other hand, was a non-factor in large part due to some excellent punting from Seattle’s Michael Dickson. | Grade: A-

item.title: Chargers fall to the Cardinals in the season opener
item.description: The AFC West watch is on. Looking at the Week 1 schedule, many expected the Los Angeles Chargers to defeat the Arizona Cardinals. On paper, the Chargers are the more talented team, they have quarterback Justin Herbert, and Mike McDaniels running their offense. This should have been a layup Week 1 win for the offseason […]
item.content:encoded:
The AFC West watch is on.

Looking at the Week 1 schedule, many expected the Los Angeles Chargers to defeat the Arizona Cardinals. On paper, the Chargers are the more talented team, they have quarterback Justin Herbert, and Mike McDaniels running their offense. This should have been a layup Week 1 win for the offseason favorites.

But that’s not what happened.

Not only did the Chargers lose to the Cardinals at home, but they were also thoroughly outplayed by first-time head coach Mike LaFleur’s squad. The worst part for the Chargers is that this was supposed to be the easy part of their schedule.

The Chargers have a home date vs. their AFC West rivals, the Las Vegas Raiders, next week in a game they will be favored to win. However, if they had issues with the Cardinals, they could struggle with the Raiders, who looked pretty decent against a bad Miami Dolphins team on Sunday. After the Raiders game is when the Chargers go through a brutal stretch of games that will frankly define their 2026 season.

They start this stretch of games with back-to-back road games in Buffalo at New Highmark Stadium vs. Josh Allen and the explosive Bills offense. Then, they head to Seattle, where the 12s will be loud to take on the defending Super Bowl Champion Seahawks. They will then head home to take on the reigning AFC West Champion Denver Broncos before going on the road again to take on the Chiefs and Rams. It doesn’t stop there, they will then host the Houston Texans and their elite defense, followed by a road date vs. Lamar Jackson and the Baltimore Ravens.

A lot has been made about the Broncos start of the season, and it is a tough one on paper, but the Chargers schedule is equally, if not more difficult. An upset loss to the lowly Cardinals who many have penciled in for a top 5 pick in next April’s NFL Draft is not the start they wanted.

The Broncos have to handle their own business starting tonight in Arrowhead vs. the returning Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs. If they can do that, they can put a game between them and the Chiefs and Chargers and be competing with….the Las Vegas Raiders…for control of the AFC West early on in the 2026 NFL season.

item.title: Broncos vs. Chiefs Monday Night Football betting odds, picks and predictions: Best bets, player props
item.description: Our NFL handicapper break downs his favorite bets in the Broncos-Chiefs Monday Night Football matchup.
item.content:encoded:
Week 1 wraps up with maybe its most high-leverage matchup, as the long-time AFC West super-power (Kansas City) takes on last season's division champ (Denver) — the only matchup between the top-two choices in a divisional betting market (especially after the Chargers were upset on Sunday). 

That Patrick Mahomes is returning from a knee injury which put the final nail in the Chiefs' 2025 season adds some intrigue against a Broncos team that might have been an injury to their own quarterback away from making the Super Bowl. 

Despite Kansas City's down year, and Denver's status as the No. 1 seed in the AFC last season, the betting market is still favoring the Chiefs, even before a couple points have been applied for a Monday night in Arrowhead.

Denver Broncos at Kansas City Chiefs (-2.5, 43.5)

Let's start with a low-level anthropological study of sharp sports bettors. 

If at any point after this line opened in mid-May, you officially decided to bet on the Broncos, and saw the line at +2.5, so close to the key number of +3, with a popular team known to take money like the Chiefs, why wouldn't you wait all summer long to see if bookmakers felt compelled to bump it up to +3? 

It's entirely possible that we're all sitting around waiting to make a bet on the Broncos at the best number available, and if we're all trying to be patient, then there isn't enough Denver money coming in to move this game closer to pick-em. 

On the field, if any quarterback is coming back from a significant knee injury (or even if one that isn't), you might expect the betting market would think it's crucial that his blindside is adequately protected. Yet, last week's news of left tackle Josh Simmons being out for Monday night, with a rookie starting in his place, still didn't trigger a move towards the Broncos. Again, potentially, because we're all waiting for +3.  

Well, hours before kickoff, we're running low on time.

Bet the Denver Broncos to cover the spread at sportsbooks

When Mahomes went down last season, the Chiefs weren't better than the Broncos. And with a defensive front that can take advantage of Simmons' absence and stuff Kansas City's alleged commitment to a run game with Kenneth Walker, Kansas City isn't better than Denver now. 

If this game doesn't drift down to pick-em by kickoff, I'll be surprised, as that would be a mistake. 

Bet: Broncos +2.5

Player props

WR Jaylen Waddle over 52.5 receiving yards (-115, Bet365)

We didn't mention the matchup of the Broncos' offense against the Chiefs defense, because we were saving that handicap for our player prop section. Denver made a point to go out and get Jaylen Waddle, and I'll be shocked if Sean Payton doesn't make a point to use him constantly this season to take even more pressure off of Bo Nix. 

Two quality corners went from the Chiefs to the Rams in the offseason, and that's probably a necessary move in the long term for Kansas City to manage its salary cap. However, hoping first-round pick Mansoor Delane plays at a high level from Game 1, and that L'Jarius Sneed turns back the clock the second time around in K.C. seems perilous in a tough matchup. Especially, with a pass-rush mitigated by one of the best offensive lines in the league. 

QB Patrick Mahomes under 229.5 passing yards (-115, Bet365)

Here's a derivative way to play on a shaky performance from Mahomes, coming off of injury and with a rookie protecting his blind side. Also, the Chiefs still haven't answered a lack of explosiveness and depth in their receiving corps, and Patrick Surtain II should have his usual one-half of the field locked down. 

RB Brashard Smith over 12.5 rushing + receiving yards (-115, Bet365)

Through thick-and-thin last season, Brashard Smith was a pet props project of ours over at THE WINDOW, as a quasi-gadget player out of the Chiefs' backfield, capable of turning a few touches into big plays. 

Before Mahomes' injury, Smith had at least three touches in a six-of-seven game stretch. In this second season, more should be on Smith's plate for an offense that he was added to late in the 2025 draft because it has lacked explosiveness. 

Anytime touchdown scorers

WR Jaylen Waddle (+210, DraftKings) 

See above, for why Waddle will be a part of the overall game plan, as his speed allows for a possible short throw that turns into a long gain. 

TE Evan Engram (+475, DraftKings)

Engram scored just one touchdown in his first season with the Broncos, despite 50 catches in the regular season on 76 targets. In 2024, all Denver tight ends combined had 51 receptions on 70 targets, but they had five touchdowns in Payton's offense. 

With the assumption of at least the usual workload in this role, we should expect an Engram touchdown around a quarter of the time, making fair odds closer to +300.

WR Rashee Rice (+155, Bet365)

Rice came off suspension last season, and was immediately a red-zone weapon, with two touchdowns on quick tosses designed for him. With six touchdowns overall, Rice scored in half his eight games played in 2025, after scoring in two of four games played in 2024. Scoring 50% of the time implies even-money odds, so anything better than +150 is worth a look, even on the side we're against for the game as a whole. 

You can find more valuable betting analysis from Yahoo Sports betting contributor, Matt Russell, at THE WINDOW.

item.title: This NFL special teams play should be shown to every high school football team
item.description: Commanders defender Tyler Owens delivered the best special teams play of NFL Week 1
item.content:encoded:
Life as a punt gunner can be hard in football, and particularly in the NFL.

The basic job description reads like something out of “American Gladiators.” Sprint 50 to 60 yards downfield while tracking a punt and either tackle one of the more elusive players on the opposing team after they field it, or have the awareness to track the football in flight, see where it lands, and touch it down inside the opponent’s five-yard line.

And if you botch either of those, not only will you become a meme overnight, but you will definitely hear about it in Monday’s film review session.

Oh, and adding to the difficulty is that you will often be up against at least one, sometimes two, players on the other side of the ball, trying their best to prevent you from even getting ten yards downfield.

That is what faced Washington Commanders safety Tyler Owens in the second quarter of Sunday’s loss to the Philadelphia Eagles. The Commanders faced a 4th and 19, and brought the punt team into the game.

Owens aligned to the right side of the punt formation, with a pair of Eagles across from him.

He would not be denied:

Not only does Owens fight through the double-team, but he finishes off the play with a thunderous tackle on Eagles returner Britain Covey, in a move pulled from the infamous charity fight between another Philadelphia legend, Rocky Balboa, and Thunderlips.

Here is a tracking shot of the effort from Owens, from the NFL’s social media channel:

The Commanders fell short against the Eagles, losing by a final score of 24-22.

But on this play, Owens stood tall. Very tall.

The Las Vegas Raiders took care of business in Week 1 and are technically in sole possession of first place in the AFC West right now. The Denver Broncos and Kansas City Chiefs play tonight on Monday Night Football, while the Los Angeles Chargers suffered a major upset, leading us into this week’s AFC West roundup.

Score: 26-14, LAC loses

  • QB Justin Herbert: 17/27 (63.0%), 209 yards, 1 TD, 1 INT, 5 rushes, 29 yards
  • RB Omarion Hampton: 12 carries, 43 yards, 1 TD
  • WR Ladd McConkey: 5 catches, 82 yards, 1 TD
  • S Derwin James Jr.: 10 tackles, 1 PD
  • LB Daiyan Henley: 8 tackles, 0.5 sack

Los Angeles entered this game as 8.5-point favorites and ended up losing by double digits. It was a game filled with mistakes from Jim Harbaugh’s crew, with a couple of turnovers (a fumble by Hampton in addition to the Herbert interception noted above) and a blocked punt that led to a two-possession fourth-quarter lead for Arizona. The Cardinals even had a missed field goal and 111 yards in penalties, and still managed to pull off the major upset.

Defensively, Los Angeles had no answer for Arizona’s passing game. Quarterback Jacob Brissett went 27-for-37 and put up 277 yards and a touchdown with no interceptions, while tight end Trey McBride accounted for nine catches, 95 yards and a score. That sets up a big Week 2 matchup between the Raiders and Chargers, as the Silver and Black can really push one of their rivals down the division standings with a win.
